empires.summary: In 962 the German king Otto I was crowned emperor by the pope in Rome, renewing Charlemagne's imperial title. The resulting empire, called Holy Roman from the 12th century, joined the German lands with northern Italy and Burgundy, and later Bohemia. Its emperors were elected by leading princes, a system fixed by the Golden Bull of 1356. Emperors clashed with the papacy over control of the Church and with Italian cities over taxes, and real power steadily passed to hundreds of princes, bishops and free cities. From 1438 the Habsburgs held the title almost continuously, and Charles V ruled a vast domain, but the Reformation and the Thirty Years War left the empire a loose federation. Napoleon's victories led Francis II to dissolve it in 1806.
empires.legacy: The empire's layered, federal style of government shaped Germany, Austria and central Europe, though Voltaire quipped it was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.

empires.summary: When the last Carolingian king of West Francia died in 987, the nobles elected Hugh Capet, whose family directly ruled only a small region around Paris. Over the next three centuries the Capetian kings steadily extended royal power over the great dukes and counts, and Philip II Augustus took Normandy and other lands from the English Angevin kings. The Hundred Years War with England, from 1337, nearly broke the kingdom until Joan of Arc helped revive the cause of Charles VII and the English were expelled by 1453. Under the Bourbon dynasty France became Europe's leading power, and Louis XIV ruled as an absolute monarch from Versailles. Debt, inequality and Enlightenment ideas fuelled the Revolution of 1789, and the monarchy was abolished in 1792.
empires.legacy: The French monarchy built one of Europe's first centralised nation-states, and its overthrow launched the age of modern revolutions.

empires.summary: The Kingdom of England was created when Æthelstan of Wessex, building on his grandfather Alfred the Great's resistance to the Vikings, brought all the English kingdoms under his rule in 927. After conquest by the Danish king Cnut in 1016 and William of Normandy in 1066, England was tied to French lands, and under Henry II it formed the core of the Angevin realm stretching to the Pyrenees. Kings shared power with barons, as in Magna Carta of 1215, and from the 13th century with Parliament. England fought the Hundred Years War against France, lost its French territories and endured the Wars of the Roses. The Tudors broke with Rome and ruled Ireland as a kingdom. In 1707 England united with Scotland to form Great Britain.
empires.legacy: Medieval England developed the common law, Magna Carta and Parliament, institutions later spread worldwide by the British Empire.

empires.summary: Kievan Rus grew from settlements of Scandinavian traders and warriors, known as the Rus or Varangians, along the river routes linking the Baltic to the Black Sea and Byzantium. According to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg of Novgorod seized Kyiv in 882 and made it his capital, ruling over East Slavic, Finnic and Baltic peoples. The Rurikid princes collected tribute in furs and slaves and traded with Constantinople, which they also raided. In 988 Vladimir the Great accepted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium, and his son Yaroslav the Wise issued a law code and built St Sophia's Cathedral. After 1054 the realm fragmented into rival principalities ruled by branches of the dynasty. The Mongol invasion destroyed it, and Kyiv was sacked in 1240.
empires.legacy: Kievan Rus is claimed as the shared cradle of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus, and gave them Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic literary tradition.

empires.name: Bulgarian Empire
empires.capital: Pliska, then Preslav and Ohrid; Tarnovo in the Second Empire

rulers.name: Ivan Shishman

empires.summary: The Bulgars were a Turkic people from the steppes north of the Black Sea. In 681, after defeating a Byzantine army, their khan Asparukh founded a state south of the Danube, where the Bulgars merged with the Slavic population. Khan Krum defeated and killed a Byzantine emperor in 811, and Boris I adopted Christianity in 864, after which Bulgarian scholars developed the Cyrillic alphabet. Under Simeon I, who took the title tsar, Bulgaria dominated the Balkans and rivalled Byzantium. Basil II conquered it by 1018 after decades of war. A revolt in 1185 founded the Second Bulgarian Empire with its capital at Tarnovo, which flourished under Ivan Asen II but later fragmented. The Ottomans took Tarnovo in 1393 and the last stronghold, Vidin, in 1396.
empires.legacy: Medieval Bulgaria spread Slavonic literacy and the Cyrillic alphabet, now used by some 250 million people.

empires.name: Kingdom of Hungary
empires.capital: Esztergom and Székesfehérvár, then Buda; Pozsony (Bratislava) 1536 – 1783

peak.note: Lands of the Hungarian Crown, including Croatia-Slavonia, within Austria-Hungary

rulers.name: Árpád
rulers.note: Led the Magyar conquest of the Carpathian Basin

rulers.name: Stephen I
rulers.note: First king; converted Hungary to Christianity

rulers.name: Béla IV
rulers.note: Rebuilt the kingdom after the Mongol invasion

rulers.name: Louis I the Great
rulers.note: Also king of Poland; height of medieval power

rulers.name: Matthias Corvinus
rulers.note: Renaissance king who took Vienna

rulers.name: Louis II
rulers.note: Killed fighting the Ottomans at Mohács

rulers.name: Franz Joseph I
rulers.note: Crowned king of Hungary in the Dual Monarchy

empires.summary: The Magyars, horse-riding nomads speaking a Finno-Ugric language, crossed the Carpathians around 895 under Grand Prince Árpád and settled the Danube basin, raiding deep into Europe until their defeat at Lechfeld in 955. Árpád's descendant Stephen converted to Latin Christianity and was crowned king in 1000, founding a kingdom organised into counties around royal castles. Hungary joined with Croatia in 1102, survived the devastating Mongol invasion of 1241, and under the Angevin king Louis the Great and the Renaissance ruler Matthias Corvinus became a great power of central Europe. After the Ottomans killed King Louis II at Mohács in 1526 the kingdom was split; the Habsburgs inherited the crown and later reconquered the whole country. Hungary gained equal status within Austria-Hungary in 1867, until the monarchy collapsed in 1918.
empires.legacy: Hungary preserved a distinct Magyar language and identity in the heart of Europe and served for centuries as Christendom's frontier against the Ottomans.

empires.name: Kingdom of Poland

peak.note: Jagiellonian Poland together with Lithuania in personal union; Poland-Lithuania c. 1.1M km² c. 1480 (Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006)

rulers.name: Mieszko I
rulers.note: Accepted Christianity in 966

rulers.name: Bolesław I the Brave
rulers.note: Crowned first king of Poland in 1025

rulers.name: Casimir III the Great
rulers.note: Rebuilt the kingdom and founded Kraków University

rulers.name: Jadwiga
rulers.note: Queen whose marriage to Jogaila united Poland and Lithuania

rulers.name: Władysław II Jagiełło
rulers.note: Defeated the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald

rulers.name: Sigismund II Augustus
rulers.note: Created the Commonwealth by the Union of Lublin

empires.summary: Poland emerged under the Piast dynasty, whose duke Mieszko I accepted Christianity in 966; his son Bolesław the Brave was crowned the first king in 1025. After 1138 the realm split into duchies for nearly two centuries and suffered Mongol raids, until Władysław the Short reunited it and his son Casimir the Great rebuilt it, founding the University of Kraków and welcoming Jewish settlers. In 1386 Queen Jadwiga married Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, creating a personal union under the Jagiellonian dynasty. The union crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410 and became one of the largest states in Europe. Power gradually shifted to the nobility through the Sejm, and in 1569 the Union of Lublin turned the partnership into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
empires.legacy: Medieval Poland anchored Latin Christianity in east-central Europe and pioneered a parliamentary noble democracy that later produced Europe's first modern written constitution in 1791.

sources.title: Turchin, Adams & Hall (2006), East-West Orientation of Historical Empires, Journal of World-Systems Research 12(2), Table 1

empires.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

rulers.name: Algirdas

empires.summary: Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe. Facing the crusading Teutonic Knights, Baltic tribes united under Mindaugas in the 1230s; he was briefly crowned a Christian king in 1253. Gediminas made Vilnius his capital in the early 14th century, and he and his son Algirdas expanded south-east into the lands of the former Kievan Rus, weakened by the Mongols, so that most of the grand duchy's subjects were Orthodox Slavs. In 1386 Grand Duke Jogaila became king of Poland and accepted Catholic baptism for Lithuania. His cousin Vytautas ruled Lithuania at its greatest extent, stretching to the Black Sea. Union with Poland deepened into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569, which was partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria by 1795.
empires.legacy: Lithuania built one of medieval Europe's largest states, and its multi-faith, multilingual tradition shaped modern Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine.

empires.name: Republic of Venice

peak.note: Mainland territories in north-east Italy plus Dalmatia, Crete, Cyprus and Aegean islands

empires.summary: Venice was founded by people fleeing barbarian invasions to the islands of a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic. Traditionally its first doge, or duke, was elected in 697, and the city gradually broke free from Byzantine rule. Venice grew rich as the middleman between Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, trading spices, silk and slaves. Its merchant aristocracy governed through an elected doge, a Great Council and the powerful Council of Ten, a system that proved remarkably stable. In 1204 Doge Enrico Dandolo diverted the Fourth Crusade to sack Constantinople, giving Venice a chain of colonies including Crete. Venice later conquered a mainland empire in northern Italy, but Ottoman wars and new ocean trade routes eroded its power, and Napoleon ended the republic in 1797.
empires.legacy: Venice was a model of republican government and commerce, and its art, architecture and canals made it one of the world's most celebrated cities.

empires.name: Grand Duchy of Moscow (Muscovy)

peak.note: At the death of Vasili III, after absorbing Novgorod, Tver and Pskov; already c. 2.5M km² by 1505

empires.summary: Moscow was a minor town when Daniel, youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, received it around 1263. Its princes rose by serving the Mongol Golden Horde as tax collectors; Ivan I gained the title of grand prince and persuaded the head of the Russian Church to settle in Moscow. Dmitry Donskoy defeated a Mongol army at Kulikovo in 1380, showing the Horde could be beaten. Ivan III annexed the rich republic of Novgorod in 1478, ended tribute to the Horde after the stand on the Ugra river in 1480, married a Byzantine princess and adopted the double-headed eagle. His son Vasili III completed the gathering of the Russian lands. In 1547 Ivan IV was crowned tsar, turning the grand duchy into the Tsardom of Russia.
empires.legacy: Muscovy was the nucleus of the Russian state, which grew into the largest country in the world.

empires.capital: Córdoba (with the palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra)

peak.note: Most of the Iberian Peninsula plus parts of North Africa under al-Mansur; c. 0.6M km² c. 1000 (Taagepera 1997)

empires.summary: When the Abbasids massacred the Umayyad family in 750, the young prince Abd al-Rahman escaped to Spain and seized Córdoba in 756, founding an independent emirate in al-Andalus. His successors governed a diverse society of Arabs, Berbers, Muslim converts, Christians and Jews, and Córdoba grew into western Europe's largest and most sophisticated city, with its Great Mosque, libraries and paved, lit streets. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph, rivalling the Fatimids and Abbasids. Under him and the powerful chamberlain al-Mansur, who raided the Christian north and sacked Santiago de Compostela, the caliphate dominated Iberia. After al-Mansur's sons died, civil war broke out in 1009, and the caliphate was abolished in 1031, splitting into small rival kingdoms called taifas.
empires.legacy: Umayyad Córdoba was a beacon of learning, poetry and architecture whose Great Mosque still stands, and through al-Andalus much classical and Arabic knowledge reached Christian Europe.

empires.capital: Pasargadae, Susa, Persepolis, Ecbatana and Babylon

empires.summary: Cyrus the Great, king of the Persians in south-west Iran, overthrew his Median overlords in 550 BCE and went on to conquer Lydia and Babylon, creating the largest empire the world had yet seen. His son Cambyses added Egypt, and Darius I extended it to the Indus and into Europe. Darius organised the empire into provinces called satrapies, each paying set tribute, linked by the Royal Road and a fast courier service, and introduced standard gold coinage. The Persians generally tolerated local religions and customs, and Cyrus allowed exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem. Attempts to conquer Greece failed at Marathon and Salamis. Weakened by court intrigue and revolts, the empire fell to Alexander the Great, and Darius III was murdered in 330 BCE.
empires.legacy: The Achaemenids created the model of a tolerant, well-organised world empire, and Persepolis remains a symbol of Iranian identity.

empires.summary: The Parthians were an Iranian nomadic people, the Parni, who settled in the province of Parthia south-east of the Caspian Sea. Their leader Arsaces I founded the Arsacid dynasty around 247 BCE and, about 238 BCE, seized Parthia from its rebel Seleucid governor Andragoras. Mithridates I conquered Media and Mesopotamia, and by about 100 BCE Parthia stretched from the Euphrates to Afghanistan, controlling the overland Silk Road between Rome and China. The empire was decentralised, with great noble families and vassal kings holding much power, and its armoured cavalry and horse archers were formidable: at Carrhae in 53 BCE they destroyed a Roman army under Crassus. For nearly three centuries Parthia and Rome fought over Armenia and Mesopotamia. Weakened by Roman invasions and civil wars, the last king, Artabanus IV, was overthrown by the Persian Ardashir in 224.
empires.legacy: Parthia was Rome's great eastern rival for three centuries and kept Silk Road trade flowing; the Parthian shot, a backward arrow fired while retreating, survives as an English expression.

sources.title: Turchin, Adams & Hall (2006), East-West Orientation of Historical Empires, Journal of World-Systems Research 12(2), Table 1

empires.summary: Ardashir, a Persian ruler from Fars in south-west Iran, overthrew the last Parthian king in 224 and founded the Sasanian dynasty, which saw itself as heir to the Achaemenids. The Sasanians built a more centralised state than the Parthians, with Zoroastrianism as an official religion, a powerful priesthood and strong armoured cavalry. Shapur I defeated Gordian III, forced Philip the Arab to buy peace and captured Valerian in 260. For four centuries Persia was the equal of Rome and then Byzantium, fighting over Armenia, Mesopotamia and the Caucasus. Khosrow I reformed taxes and patronised learning. Khosrow II briefly conquered Egypt and the Levant, but a Byzantine counter-attack and civil war exhausted the empire. Arab Muslim armies defeated it at al-Qadisiyya and Nahavand, and the last shah, Yazdegerd III, was killed in 651.
empires.legacy: Sasanian art, court culture and administration deeply influenced the Islamic caliphates, Byzantium and lands as far away as China.

empires.summary: Around 322 BCE Chandragupta Maurya, reportedly guided by the minister Chanakya (Kautilya), overthrew the Nanda kings of Magadha in the Ganges valley. Moving into the vacuum left by Alexander's withdrawal, he conquered the north-west and later won Afghan territory from Seleucus I. His son Bindusara pushed south, and his grandson Ashoka conquered Kalinga in a war so bloody that he turned to Buddhism. Ashoka promoted dhamma, a code of non-violence, tolerance and welfare, carved in edicts on rocks and pillars across the empire, and sent Buddhist missionaries abroad. The Mauryas ruled through a large bureaucracy, spies and a standing army, as described in the Arthashastra. After Ashoka the empire shrank, and in about 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last emperor.
empires.legacy: The Mauryas first unified most of the Indian subcontinent, and Ashoka's lion capital and wheel are now India's national emblem and the symbol on its flag.

empires.summary: The Kushans descended from the Yuezhi, nomads driven from western China by the Xiongnu, who settled in Bactria (northern Afghanistan) in the 2nd century BCE. In the 1st century CE Kujula Kadphises united the five Yuezhi clans and crossed the Hindu Kush into northern India. Under Kanishka, the most famous ruler, the empire reached from Central Asia across Gandhara to the Ganges valley. Sitting astride the Silk Road, the Kushans grew rich on trade between Rome, Parthia, India and China, and their gold coins show Greek, Persian, Indian and local gods side by side. Kanishka patronised Buddhism, and Gandhara art blended Greek and Indian styles. From the 3rd century the Sasanians conquered the western lands, and the remaining Kushan principalities faded by the late 4th century.
empires.legacy: The Kushans helped carry Buddhism along the Silk Road to China, and Gandhara art produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form.

empires.summary: The Gupta dynasty rose in the Ganges valley, and Chandragupta I took the title great king of kings around 320. His son Samudragupta campaigned across the subcontinent, defeating northern kings and forcing southern rulers to pay tribute, and Chandragupta II added western India. The Guptas ruled the heartland directly and controlled outer regions through vassals. Their era is often called India's classical age: Sanskrit literature flourished with the poet Kalidasa, Aryabhata calculated the Earth's rotation and used a place-value number system, and Hindu temple architecture took shape, while Buddhist monasteries such as Nalanda thrived. From the late 5th century invasions by the Alchon Huns, together with the rise of regional rulers, broke up the empire by about 550.
empires.legacy: The Gupta age set enduring standards in Indian art, literature, mathematics and astronomy, and the decimal numerals it refined reached the world through Arab scholars.

empires.summary: The Cholas were one of the three ancient Tamil ruling families of southern India, mentioned in Ashoka's edicts and in early Tamil Sangam poetry. After centuries in the shadow of the Pallavas and Pandyas, Vijayalaya revived the dynasty around 848 by capturing Thanjavur. Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra I built an empire covering southern India and Sri Lanka, sent an army to the Ganges and launched a naval expedition against Srivijaya in 1025, projecting power across the Bay of Bengal. The Cholas ran an efficient administration with self-governing village assemblies, promoted trade with China and South-east Asia, and built great Shiva temples such as the Brihadeeswarar at Thanjavur. Wars with the Chalukyas and Pandyas weakened them, and the Pandyas ended the dynasty in 1279.
empires.legacy: Chola bronzes, temples and maritime trade spread Tamil culture across South-east Asia, and their great temples remain living places of worship.

empires.summary: After Muhammad of Ghor conquered northern India, his Turkic slave-general Qutb ud-Din Aibak made himself sultan at Delhi in 1206. Five dynasties followed: the Mamluks, Khaljis, Tughluqs, Sayyids and Lodis. The sultans ruled through a Turkic and Afghan military elite granted revenue rights over land, and they repelled repeated Mongol invasions. Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq pushed deep into southern India, briefly ruling most of the subcontinent, but rebellions created independent states such as the Bahmani and Vijayanagara kingdoms. Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 left the sultanate a regional power. Persian became the language of government, and Indo-Islamic architecture such as the Qutb Minar flourished. Babur defeated the last sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, at Panipat in 1526, founding the Mughal Empire.
empires.legacy: The sultanate established Islam as a lasting force in South Asia and fostered the blending of cultures that produced the Urdu language and Indo-Islamic architecture.

empires.summary: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty, in the wake of the Delhi Sultanate's raids into southern India. From their capital on the Tungabhadra river they united the Hindu kingdoms of the south, and for two centuries fought the Bahmani sultanate and its successors for the fertile Raichur Doab. Under Krishnadevaraya the empire covered almost all of India south of the Krishna river. Its capital was one of the largest and richest cities in the world, admired by Persian and Portuguese visitors for its markets, temples and waterworks. Revenue came from land and a busy trade in horses, spices and cotton. In 1565 the allied Deccan sultanates crushed its army at Talikota and sacked the capital, and the empire lingered in decline until 1646.
empires.legacy: The ruins of Hampi are a World Heritage Site, and Vijayanagara patronage helped preserve and develop South Indian music, literature and temple architecture.

empires.summary: After the murder of the fourth caliph Ali, Muawiya, governor of Syria and a member of the Meccan Umayyad clan, became caliph in 661 and made the office hereditary. Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyads continued the Arab conquests on an enormous scale: North Africa, Spain, Transoxiana and Sindh were all taken by the early 8th century, creating one of the largest empires in history. Abd al-Malik made Arabic the language of government, introduced Islamic coinage and built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Arab Muslims formed a privileged ruling class, which angered non-Arab converts and supporters of Ali's family. A revolt that began in Khurasan in 747 led to the dynasty's overthrow by the Abbasids in 750, although one prince escaped to found an Umayyad emirate in Spain.
empires.legacy: The Umayyads spread Islam and the Arabic language from the Atlantic to India, laying the foundations of the Islamic world.

sources.title: Taagepera (1997), Expansion and Contraction Patterns of Large Polities

empires.summary: The Abbasids, descendants of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas, overthrew the Umayyads in 750 with support from Persian converts in Khurasan. Their second caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad, which became one of the world's largest cities. The Abbasid state adopted Persian-style court ceremony and a bureaucracy run by viziers, and its early centuries were a golden age: under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian works and advanced mathematics, astronomy and medicine. From the 9th century the caliphs relied on Turkish slave soldiers, and provinces broke away under local dynasties. From 945 the Buyids and then the Seljuks held real power in Baghdad. The Mongols under Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed the last caliph, al-Musta'sim.
empires.legacy: Abbasid scholars preserved and built on ancient learning, giving the world algebra, algorithms and much of the science later passed on to Europe.

empires.summary: The Seljuks were a clan of Oghuz Turks from the steppes east of the Aral Sea who converted to Sunni Islam. Led by the brothers Tughril and Chaghri, they defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 and swept into Iran, and Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055 as protector of the Abbasid caliph, who named him sultan. His nephew Alp Arslan crushed the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement, and under Malik-Shah and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk the empire stretched from the Mediterranean to Central Asia, with madrasas spreading Sunni learning. After 1092 it fragmented among rival princes, and the eastern branch collapsed after Sanjar's death. A branch in Anatolia, the Sultanate of Rum, flourished at Konya until the Mongols made it a vassal in 1243; it vanished around 1308.
empires.legacy: The Seljuks brought Turkish peoples into the heart of the Middle East and Anatolia, preparing the way for the Ottomans, and their victories over Byzantium helped trigger the Crusades.

empires.summary: The Ilkhanate was the Mongol khanate in Iran, founded by Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, who was sent west by his brother, the Great Khan Möngke. Hulagu destroyed the fortresses of the Assassins and sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate, but his advance into Syria was stopped by the Mamluks in 1260. The Ilkhans ruled Iran, Iraq, the Caucasus and Anatolia, fought the Golden Horde and the Mamluks, and exchanged embassies with the pope and European kings. In 1295 Ghazan converted to Islam and, with his vizier Rashid al-Din, reformed taxation and patronised learning; Rashid al-Din's world history is a landmark. Ilkhanid Tabriz became a hub of trade and art linking China and the west. When Abu Sa'id died without an heir in 1335, the khanate collapsed into rival successor states.
empires.legacy: The Ilkhanate reconnected Iran with China, blending Persian and Chinese art and shaping the later tradition of Persian miniature painting.

empires.summary: Timur, known in Europe as Tamerlane, was a Turkic-Mongol warlord from Transoxiana who made himself master of the western Chagatai lands in 1370. Claiming to restore Genghis Khan's empire, though he ruled through puppet khans and called himself emir, he spent 35 years campaigning: he devastated Iran, crushed the Golden Horde, sacked Delhi in 1398 and defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402. His conquests were brutal, marked by towers of skulls, but he filled Samarkand with captured craftsmen and splendid buildings. After his death in 1405, while marching on China, his son Shah Rukh held the core together from Herat, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built a famous observatory. The empire then splintered among princes and fell to the Uzbeks and Safavids by 1507.
empires.legacy: The Timurid courts at Samarkand and Herat sparked a brilliant flowering of Persian art, architecture and science, and Timur's descendant Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

empires.summary: The Ottomans began as one of many small Turkish principalities in north-west Anatolia, led around 1299 by Osman, from whom the dynasty takes its name. Combining frontier warfare against Byzantium with skilful alliances, his successors expanded into the Balkans, and in 1453 Mehmed II captured Constantinople. Selim I conquered the Mamluk lands of Syria, Egypt and Arabia, and under Suleiman the Magnificent the empire reached Hungary and dominated the eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea. The sultans ruled a multi-ethnic, multi-faith realm through a slave-based elite, including the Janissary infantry, and allowed religious communities to manage their own affairs. From the late 17th century the empire lost territory to Austria and Russia and, despite modernising reforms, was dismantled after defeat in the First World War; the sultanate was abolished in 1922.
empires.legacy: For six centuries the Ottomans linked Europe, Asia and Africa, and their legacy shapes the borders, cuisines and politics of the Balkans and the Middle East today.

empires.summary: The Xiongnu were a confederation of nomadic peoples on the Mongolian steppe. In 209 BCE Modu killed his father Touman and made himself chanyu, or supreme ruler, uniting the tribes into the first great steppe empire. Modu defeated the Donghu and Yuezhi, and in 200 BCE trapped the founder of the Han dynasty at Baideng, forcing China into treaties that sent silk, grain and princesses as brides to the steppe. The Xiongnu state was a hierarchy of tribal leaders under the chanyu's clan, relying on mounted archers and control of trade. From 133 BCE Emperor Wu of Han launched long wars that pushed them back. Civil wars split the confederation: the southern Xiongnu submitted to the Han and settled inside China, while the northern branch was crushed around 89 to 91 CE.
empires.legacy: The Xiongnu set the pattern for later steppe empires and for China's frontier policy, and their pressure spurred early Great Wall building and the opening of the Silk Road.

empires.summary: The Göktürks, or Celestial Turks, were metal-working vassals of the Rouran in the Altai Mountains. In 552 their chief Bumin rebelled, destroyed the Rouran and took the title qaghan, founding the first state to bear the name Turk. Within a generation his brother Istämi and son Muqan had built an empire stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea, controlling the Silk Road and negotiating with Byzantium, Persia and China. The empire split into eastern and western khaganates around 582, and both fell under Tang Chinese control in the 630s and 650s. In 682 Ilterish revived the eastern khaganate, which reached its height under Bilge Qaghan. Internal strife and an uprising by the Uyghurs, Basmyls and Karluks ended the khaganate in 744.
empires.legacy: The Göktürks gave their name to the Turkic peoples, and the Orkhon inscriptions are the oldest known texts in a Turkic language.

empires.summary: The Tibetan Empire was forged in the early 7th century when Namri Songtsen and his son Songtsen Gampo, kings of the Yarlung valley, united the clans of the Tibetan plateau. Songtsen Gampo founded Lhasa, married Nepalese and Chinese princesses, and is credited with introducing Buddhism and a writing system adapted from Indian scripts. Tibetan armies became a major military power: they fought Tang China for control of the Silk Road oasis cities of the Tarim Basin, and in 763 briefly captured the Tang capital, Chang'an. Under Trisong Detsen Buddhism became the state religion and the first monastery, Samye, was built. A peace treaty with China was carved in stone in 822. After the assassination of King Langdarma around 842, succession disputes broke the empire apart.
empires.legacy: The empire unified Tibet's language and identity and planted the Buddhist tradition that has defined Tibetan civilisation ever since.

empires.summary: In 1206 an assembly of steppe tribes proclaimed Temüjin as Genghis Khan, ruler of all the Mongols. Reorganising his followers into units of tens, hundreds and thousands loyal to him rather than to their clans, he created a disciplined army of mounted archers that conquered northern China, Central Asia and parts of Persia. His sons and grandsons continued the expansion: Ögedei finished off the Jin dynasty, Batu overran Russia and invaded Poland and Hungary, Hulagu took Baghdad, and Kublai conquered the Song. The Mongols ruled through local officials, a postal relay system and religious tolerance, and their peace made Eurasian trade routes safer than ever. After Möngke's death in 1259 the empire split into four khanates, and Mongol rule in China ended in 1368.
empires.legacy: The Mongol Empire connected East and West as never before, spreading goods, technologies and ideas, and also the Black Death, across Eurasia.

empires.summary: The Golden Horde was the north-western part of the Mongol Empire, granted to the descendants of Genghis Khan's eldest son Jochi. After his son Batu's great western campaign of 1236 to 1242 conquered the Volga Bulgars, the Kipchak steppe and the Russian principalities, Batu settled at Sarai on the lower Volga. The khans ruled the steppe directly, while Russian princes kept their thrones as tribute-paying vassals. The Horde grew rich on trade along the Volga and through Black Sea ports, and under Özbeg Khan it adopted Islam. From the 1350s it suffered plague and civil war; Tokhtamysh briefly reunited it, but Timur destroyed Sarai in 1395. It then broke into the khanates of Kazan, Crimea, Astrakhan and others, and the remnant Great Horde was destroyed in 1502.
empires.legacy: Two centuries of Horde overlordship shaped Russian political traditions, and its Turkic Muslim population included the ancestors of the Volga and Crimean Tatars and the Kazakhs.

empires.summary: The Chagatai Khanate was the Central Asian share of the Mongol Empire, given to Genghis Khan's second son Chagatai. It covered Transoxiana, the steppes of Semirechye and the oasis cities of the Tarim Basin. Its khans kept their nomadic way of life longer than the other Mongol branches, and for decades they fought the Yuan and the Ilkhanate, often in alliance with the rebel prince Kaidu. Under Kebek and Tarmashirin the khans began to settle and adopt Islam, which provoked a revolt by the eastern nomads. By the 1340s the khanate had split into a western half in Transoxiana, soon dominated by Timur, and an eastern half known as Moghulistan, where Chagatayid khans ruled until the late 17th century, when the Dzungars took the Tarim Basin.
empires.legacy: The Chagatai Turkic language, named after the khanate, became the classical literary language of Central Asia and the ancestor of modern Uzbek and Uyghur.

empires.summary: The Shang is the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by both written records and archaeology. Traditionally founded by Tang around 1600 BCE after overthrowing the Xia, it ruled the middle and lower Yellow River valley. Shang kings governed with the help of relatives and allied lords and moved their capital several times, finally settling at Yin near modern Anyang around 1300 BCE. They practised elaborate ancestor worship, and to ask the spirits about harvests, war and childbirth, diviners cracked oracle bones of turtle shell and ox bone, inscribing the questions in the earliest known Chinese writing. Shang craftsmen cast spectacular bronze vessels, and royal tombs held chariots and human sacrifices. Around 1046 BCE King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye.
empires.legacy: Shang oracle-bone script is the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, making Chinese the world's oldest continuously used writing system.

empires.summary: The Zhou, a people from the Wei valley in the west, overthrew the Shang around 1046 BCE. They justified the conquest with the idea of the Mandate of Heaven: Heaven granted the right to rule to a virtuous dynasty and withdrew it from a corrupt one. The early Western Zhou kings ruled through a feudal network, granting lands to relatives and allies who owed loyalty and military service. In 771 BCE nomadic invaders killed King You and the court moved east to Luoyi, beginning the Eastern Zhou. Royal power then faded, and during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods rival states fought for supremacy; yet this was also the age of Confucius, Laozi and the Hundred Schools of Thought. The state of Qin deposed the last Zhou king in 256 BCE.
empires.legacy: The Zhou gave China the Mandate of Heaven and the classic texts and philosophies, Confucianism and Daoism above all, that shaped East Asian civilisation for over two thousand years.

empires.summary: Qin was a frontier state in north-west China that, after the harsh Legalist reforms of the minister Shang Yang in the 4th century BCE, built the most efficient army and administration of the Warring States. Between 230 and 221 BCE its king, Ying Zheng, conquered the six rival states and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He abolished feudal lordships in favour of commanderies run by appointed officials; standardised writing, coins, weights, measures and axle widths; built roads and canals; and linked frontier walls against the Xiongnu. He also burned books and was buried with the famous Terracotta Army. His rule relied on heavy taxes, forced labour and brutal punishments, and after his death in 210 BCE revolts toppled the dynasty in 206 BCE.
empires.legacy: The Qin created the first unified Chinese empire and its centralised model of government, and probably gave China its name in many languages.

empires.summary: After the Qin collapsed, Liu Bang, a commoner turned rebel leader, defeated his rivals and founded the Han dynasty in 202 BCE. The Han kept the Qin's centralised state but softened its harsh laws, and made Confucianism the official ideology, recruiting officials partly through examinations in the classics. Emperor Wu fought the Xiongnu, sent Zhang Qian to Central Asia, helping open the Silk Road, and extended Han rule into Korea, Vietnam and the Tarim Basin. Paper, the seismograph and advances in iron-making date from this era. The usurper Wang Mang briefly interrupted the dynasty, but the Eastern Han was restored in 25 CE. Court eunuchs, land-owning clans, floods and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 then weakened it, until warlords took over and the last emperor abdicated in 220.
empires.legacy: Han rule defined Chinese identity so strongly that China's majority people still call themselves the Han.

empires.summary: For nearly three centuries after the fall of the Han, China was divided among rival northern and southern dynasties. In 581 Yang Jian, a general of the Northern Zhou, seized the throne and founded the Sui, and in 589 he conquered the southern Chen dynasty, reunifying China. As Emperor Wen he reformed the laws, redistributed land, rebuilt the bureaucracy and began selecting officials by examination. His son Emperor Yang undertook vast projects, above all the Grand Canal linking the Yellow and Yangtze rivers; he also rebuilt the Great Wall and built a new capital at Luoyang, using millions of forced labourers. His three disastrous invasions of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo drained the treasury and provoked widespread rebellion. Yang was murdered in 618, and his general Li Yuan founded the Tang.
empires.legacy: Though short-lived, the Sui reunified China and built the Grand Canal and the institutions on which the Tang golden age rested.

empires.summary: The Tang dynasty was founded in 618 by Li Yuan and consolidated by his son Taizong, one of China's most admired emperors. Tang armies extended Chinese power deep into Central Asia, and the capital Chang'an, perhaps the largest city in the world with around a million people, welcomed merchants, monks and envoys from Persia, Japan and beyond along the Silk Road. Wu Zetian, the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name, governed from 690 to 705. Poetry flourished under Li Bai and Du Fu, Buddhism spread widely and woodblock printing appeared. Under Xuanzong the An Lushan rebellion of 755 to 763 devastated the empire, after which regional military governors grew powerful. Peasant revolts, notably Huang Chao's, finished the dynasty in 907.
empires.legacy: The Tang is remembered as a golden age of Chinese culture whose laws, city planning, poetry and Buddhism shaped Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

empires.summary: In 960 the general Zhao Kuangyin seized power and founded the Song, ending half a century of division. Wary of military strongmen, the Song placed civil officials chosen by competitive examinations in charge of government, and the scholar-official class flourished. The economy boomed: rice farming expanded, cities such as Kaifeng and Hangzhou held a million people, and the Song issued the world's first government paper money. Inventions included movable type, the magnetic compass for navigation and gunpowder weapons. Militarily the Song was weaker, paying tribute to the Liao and Western Xia; in 1127 the Jurchen Jin captured Kaifeng and the court fled south, ruling as the Southern Song from Hangzhou. The Mongols under Kublai Khan conquered it, and the last boy emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279.
empires.legacy: The Song was one of the most inventive and commercially advanced societies of the pre-modern world, and its Neo-Confucian philosophy dominated East Asia for centuries.

empires.summary: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, was proclaimed Great Khan in 1260 and in 1271 declared a Chinese-style dynasty called Yuan. He built a new capital at Dadu, modern Beijing, and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279, uniting all of China under foreign rule for the first time. His invasions of Japan and South-east Asia failed. The Yuan divided society into ranked groups, with Mongols and Central Asians above northern and southern Chinese, and relied on foreigners such as Marco Polo, who claimed to have served at court. Trade flourished, paper money circulated widely and the Grand Canal was extended to Beijing. Later rulers were weak and quarrelsome, and inflation, floods and epidemics fuelled the Red Turban rebellion, which drove the Mongols back to the steppe in 1368.
empires.legacy: The Yuan made Beijing China's capital and joined China, Tibet and Mongolia under one government, a combination later claimed by the Ming and Qing.

empires.summary: Zhu Yuanzhang, a former peasant and Buddhist monk who rose to lead the Red Turban rebels, drove out the Mongols and proclaimed the Ming dynasty in 1368, ruling as the Hongwu Emperor. He rebuilt agriculture and concentrated power in the emperor's hands. The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing, built the Forbidden City and sent Admiral Zheng He on great treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa between 1405 and 1433. The Ming rebuilt the Great Wall in the form seen today, and Ming porcelain and silk were prized worldwide, drawing in vast amounts of silver from Japan and the Americas. Later emperors withdrew from government, and factional strife, war in Korea, famine and rebellion weakened the state. Rebels took Beijing in 1644, and the Manchu Qing dynasty, proclaimed by Hong Taiji in 1636, seized the throne.
empires.legacy: The Ming left the Great Wall, the Forbidden City and blue-and-white porcelain, and its silver economy tied China into the first global trade networks.

empires.summary: Goryeo was founded in 918 by Wang Geon, a general from Kaesong, who reunited Korea after the breakup of Unified Silla by 936; the modern name Korea comes from Goryeo. Its kings built a centralised state on the Chinese model with civil service examinations, while powerful aristocratic families dominated the court. Buddhism was the state religion, and Goryeo is famous for its jade-green celadon pottery and for the Tripitaka Koreana, the Buddhist scriptures carved on more than 80,000 woodblocks. The kingdom repelled Khitan invasions, but from 1170 military officers seized power. After decades of resistance it made peace with the Mongols in 1259 and became a vassal of the Yuan, with its kings marrying Yuan princesses. Weakened by pirate raids and factional strife, it was overthrown by General Yi Seong-gye in 1392.
empires.legacy: Goryeo gave Korea its name in the West and pioneered printing with movable metal type; the Jikji, printed in 1377, is the oldest surviving example.

empires.summary: General Yi Seong-gye overthrew Goryeo in 1392 and founded the Joseon dynasty, which ruled Korea for five centuries from its new capital, Hanyang, today's Seoul. Joseon adopted Neo-Confucianism as its guiding philosophy, governing through a scholar-bureaucracy selected by examinations and dominated by the yangban aristocracy, while Buddhism lost its privileges. King Sejong the Great sponsored science and in 1443 created Hangul, a simple phonetic alphabet. Joseon survived devastating Japanese invasions in 1592 to 1598, when Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships won famous victories, and Manchu invasions in the 1620s and 1630s, after which it became a tributary of the Qing and limited foreign contact, earning the name Hermit Kingdom. Forced open by Japan in 1876, it became the Korean Empire in 1897 and was annexed by Japan in 1910.
empires.legacy: Joseon shaped Korea's language, Confucian social values and national culture, and Hangul remains the Korean alphabet today.

empires.summary: From around 250 CE, the age of great keyhole-shaped burial mounds, the Yamato kings of the Nara basin gradually brought the clans of central and western Japan under their rule. Adopting Buddhism, Chinese writing and Tang-style law codes between the 6th and 8th centuries, they became emperors governing from planned capitals at Nara and, from 794, Heian-kyo, now Kyoto. In the Heian period the Fujiwara family ruled as regents for child emperors, and court culture produced masterpieces such as The Tale of Genji. Provincial warrior clans grew powerful, and after the Genpei War Minamoto no Yoritomo set up a military government, the shogunate, at Kamakura in 1185. The Kamakura regents of the Hojo family repelled Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281, but strained by the cost, the shogunate fell in 1333.
empires.legacy: This era created Japan's imperial institution, the world's oldest continuous hereditary monarchy, and the samurai culture of the shogunate.

empires.summary: In 802 Jayavarman II declared himself universal monarch in a ceremony on the Kulen hills, freeing the Khmer lands from Javanese overlordship and founding the Angkorian empire in what is now Cambodia. His successors built the city of Angkor near the Tonle Sap lake, supported by a vast system of reservoirs and canals that watered rice fields for perhaps 700,000 people. Khmer kings presented themselves as god-kings linked to Shiva or Vishnu, and later to the Buddha. Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat, the world's largest religious monument, and Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom and the Bayon and extended the empire across Thailand, Laos and southern Vietnam. From the 13th century wars with the Thai and Cham, strain on the water system and climate shifts weakened Angkor, which Ayutthaya sacked in 1431.
empires.legacy: Angkor Wat is Cambodia's national symbol and one of humanity's greatest architectural achievements.

empires.summary: Srivijaya was a maritime empire centred on Palembang in southern Sumatra, first recorded in the 670s, when the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Yijing studied Sanskrit there. Its rulers grew rich by controlling the Straits of Malacca and Sunda, the sea lanes between China and India, taxing passing ships and suppressing piracy, while drawing on Sumatran gold and forest products. Srivijaya was a federation of port-cities bound to the ruler by oaths, gifts and trade privileges rather than a tightly governed territory. It was a great centre of Mahayana Buddhism, linked with the Sailendra dynasty of Java, which built Borobudur. In 1025 the Chola navy of southern India sacked its ports, beginning a long decline. Rivalry from Javanese states and shifts in Chinese trade weakened it further, and Majapahit absorbed its remnants in the late 14th century.
empires.legacy: Srivijaya helped make Malay the common language of island South-east Asia, the root of today's Indonesian and Malay.

empires.summary: Majapahit was founded in 1293 by Raden Wijaya, a Javanese prince who cleverly used an invading Mongol army sent by Kublai Khan to defeat his rival, then turned on the Mongols and drove them out. From its capital at Trowulan in East Java the kingdom grew rich on rice farming and the spice trade. Under Queen Tribhuwana and her son Hayam Wuruk, the prime minister Gajah Mada vowed to unite the archipelago, and Majapahit claimed tribute from much of modern Indonesia, the Malay Peninsula and beyond, though it ruled directly mainly over Java, Madura and Bali. The court poem Nagarakretagama describes its splendour. After Hayam Wuruk's death, civil war, the rise of Malacca and the spread of Islamic coastal sultanates eroded its power, and it ended in the early 16th century.
empires.legacy: Majapahit is celebrated in Indonesia as a symbol of national unity, and its Hindu-Buddhist culture survives most strongly in Bali.

empires.summary: Pagan grew from a settlement on the middle Irrawaddy, traditionally fortified in 849, into the first kingdom to unite the lands that make up modern Myanmar. King Anawrahta, who came to the throne in 1044, conquered the Mon of lower Burma and adopted Theravada Buddhism, which became the faith of the Burmese people. Under him and successors such as Kyansittha and Narapatisithu, the kingdom prospered from irrigated rice farming, and kings, nobles and commoners competed to earn religious merit by building temples. More than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries rose on the plain of Pagan in about 250 years. So much land was donated tax-free to the Buddhist clergy that royal revenues shrank. Weakened, Pagan was invaded by the Mongols in 1287 and broke apart by 1297.
empires.legacy: The thousands of temples at Bagan are among Asia's great monuments, and Pagan established the Burmese language, script and Theravada Buddhism in Myanmar.

empires.summary: Northern Vietnam was ruled by China for about a thousand years until Ngô Quyền defeated a Southern Han fleet at the Bạch Đằng River in 938. In 968 Đinh Bộ Lĩnh unified the country and founded the kingdom later known as Đại Việt, Great Viet. The Lý dynasty moved the capital to Thăng Long, modern Hanoi, in 1010 and built a Confucian bureaucracy alongside Buddhism. The Trần dynasty repelled three Mongol invasions in the 13th century, and after a brief Ming occupation Lê Lợi restored independence in 1428. The Lê kings pushed steadily south at the expense of Champa. From the 16th century the realm was divided, first by the Mạc usurpation of 1527 and then between rival lords, the Trịnh in the north and Nguyễn in the south, until the Tây Sơn rebellion and the Nguyễn dynasty reunified it, renaming it Vietnam in 1804.
empires.legacy: Đại Việt forged a Vietnamese identity defined by resistance to Chinese domination and by the long march south that created the shape of modern Vietnam.

empires.summary: Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 by King U Thong, who took the title Ramathibodi I, on an island where three rivers meet in Thailand's central plain. The kingdom absorbed the older Thai state of Sukhothai and in 1431 sacked Angkor, inheriting Khmer ideas of divine kingship. Its rulers built a highly organised state, with the sakdina system ranking every subject by land and duty. Ayutthaya became one of Asia's great trading cities, home to Chinese, Persian, Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch and French merchants, and King Narai exchanged embassies with Louis XIV. For centuries it fought Burmese kingdoms; it fell to Burma in 1569, until King Naresuan restored its independence. In 1767 a Burmese army destroyed the city after a long siege, ending the kingdom.
empires.legacy: Ayutthaya shaped Thai monarchy, law and culture, and its ruins are a World Heritage Site; later Thai kingdoms saw themselves as its heirs.

empires.summary: The Olmec, who lived in the hot, swampy lowlands of Mexico's Gulf Coast in today's Veracruz and Tabasco, created the first complex society in Mesoamerica. Around 1200 BCE San Lorenzo became a major centre, with earthen platforms and drainage channels, and after about 900 BCE La Venta took its place, with a great earthen pyramid. Olmec rulers, possibly the people portrayed in the famous colossal basalt heads weighing up to about 50 tons, controlled trade in jade, obsidian and other luxury goods across Mesoamerica. The Olmec developed a religion featuring jaguar, maize and rain deities, and probably played the rubber ball game. Their own name is unknown; Olmec, meaning rubber people, is an Aztec word. The heartland declined around 400 BCE, probably because of environmental change.
empires.legacy: Often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica, the Olmec pioneered art styles, religious ideas and the ball game later developed by the Maya and others.

empires.name: Maya civilisation
empires.capital: No single capital; great cities included El Mirador, Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán, Chichén Itzá and Mayapán

peak.note: Classic-period city-states across southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and western Honduras (rough estimate)

rulers.name: K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' of Copán
rulers.note: Founder of Copán's royal dynasty

rulers.name: K'inich Janaab Pakal I of Palenque
rulers.note: Buried in the Temple of the Inscriptions

rulers.name: Yuknoom Ch'een II of Calakmul
rulers.note: Led the Kaan kingdom at its height

rulers.name: Jasaw Chan K'awiil I of Tikal
rulers.note: Revived Tikal by defeating Calakmul in 695

rulers.name: Kan Ek'
rulers.note: Itza king of Nojpetén, the last independent Maya kingdom

empires.summary: Maya farming villages appeared in southern Mexico and Central America by about 2000 BCE, and by 300 BCE great cities such as El Mirador were building huge pyramids. In the Classic period, from about 250 to 900 CE, dozens of city-states ruled by divine kings flourished in the lowland rainforest, and superpowers such as Tikal and Calakmul fought for dominance through warfare and alliances. The Maya developed the most complete writing system in the Americas, recorded dates in their Long Count calendar, tracked the movements of Venus and used the concept of zero. In the 9th century the southern cities collapsed, probably due to drought, overpopulation and constant war, but northern centres such as Chichén Itzá and Mayapán continued. The Spanish conquered most Maya states in the 16th century, and the last, Nojpetén, in 1697.
empires.legacy: Millions of Maya people still live in the region speaking Mayan languages, and their deciphered inscriptions reveal one of the ancient world's most sophisticated cultures.

sources.title: Martin & Velásquez García (2016), Polities and Places: Tracing the Toponyms of the Snake Dynasty, PARI Journal 17(2)

empires.name: Teotihuacan

peak.note: A city of perhaps 100,000 people dominating the Valley of Mexico, with influence reaching the Maya region (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Rulers unknown
rulers.note: No royal portraits or names survive; the city may have been governed by councils

rulers.name: Spearthrower Owl
rulers.note: Possible Teotihuacan ruler named in Maya inscriptions, whose son became king of Tikal

empires.summary: Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico north-east of modern Mexico City, grew from about 100 BCE into one of the largest cities in the ancient world, home to perhaps 100,000 people at its height around 450 CE. It was laid out on a grid along a great avenue, later called the Avenue of the Dead, lined with the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. Its people lived in large apartment compounds, some housing migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf Coast. Teotihuacan controlled the obsidian trade and influenced cities across Mesoamerica; in 378 its envoys intervened in the Maya city of Tikal and installed a new dynasty. Around 550 the city centre was burned, perhaps in an internal revolt, and the population dispersed.
empires.legacy: The Aztecs revered the ruined city, naming it Teotihuacan, the place where the gods were created, and it is now one of Mexico's most visited ancient sites.

empires.name: Aztec Empire (Triple Alliance)

peak.note: Tributary provinces from the Gulf Coast to the Pacific; c. 0.22M km² in 1520 (Taagepera 1997)

rulers.name: Itzcoatl
rulers.note: Formed the Triple Alliance

rulers.name: Moctezuma I
rulers.note: Expanded the empire to the Gulf Coast

rulers.name: Ahuitzotl
rulers.note: Greatest conqueror; rebuilt the Great Temple

rulers.name: Moctezuma II
rulers.note: Ruler when the Spanish arrived

rulers.name: Cuauhtémoc
rulers.note: Last emperor; defended Tenochtitlan

empires.summary: The Mexica, a people who claimed to have migrated from a homeland called Aztlan, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325. At first vassals of the Tepanec city of Azcapotzalco, in 1428 they formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan and overthrew their overlords. Under rulers such as Moctezuma I and Ahuitzotl, the alliance conquered much of central and southern Mexico, collecting tribute in maize, cotton, cacao, feathers and gold from hundreds of towns rather than governing them directly. Tenochtitlan, linked to the shore by causeways and fed by floating chinampa gardens, held perhaps 200,000 people. Warfare also supplied captives for human sacrifice. In 1519 Hernán Cortés arrived; allied with the Tlaxcalans and helped by smallpox, the Spanish captured Tenochtitlan in 1521.
empires.legacy: Mexico City stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, and the Aztec emblem of an eagle on a cactus appears on the Mexican flag.

sources.title: Taagepera (1997), Expansion and Contraction Patterns of Large Polities

empires.name: Tiwanaku

peak.note: Influence from the Titicaca basin into southern Peru, northern Chile and north-west Argentina (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Rulers unknown
rulers.note: Tiwanaku had no writing; its elite is known only from monuments such as the Gateway of the Sun

empires.summary: Tiwanaku grew near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, about 3,850 metres above sea level in what is now Bolivia. Settled long before, it became a major city and ceremonial centre from about 500 CE, with stone temples such as the Akapana pyramid, the Kalasasaya enclosure and the carved Gateway of the Sun. Its farmers fed tens of thousands of people using raised fields separated by canals, which protected crops from frost, while herds of llamas and alpacas carried goods. Tiwanaku spread its influence through colonies, religion and trade across the southern Andes into Peru, Chile and Argentina, sharing a staff-god imagery with its northern neighbour Wari. After about 1000 a long drought undermined its farming, and the city was gradually abandoned.
empires.legacy: Tiwanaku is a symbol of indigenous Andean identity in Bolivia, and its raised-field farming has been revived by modern farmers.

empires.name: Wari Empire

peak.note: Much of the Peruvian highlands and coast (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Rulers unknown
rulers.note: Wari left no writing; its rulers' names are lost

empires.summary: The Wari state rose around 600 CE in the Ayacucho valley of the central Peruvian highlands, with its capital at Huari, a city covering several square kilometres. Many archaeologists see Wari as the first true empire of the Andes: it built planned administrative centres such as Pikillacta near Cusco and Viracochapampa in the north, linked by roads, and moved colonists to expand terrace farming. Wari officials probably kept records on khipus, knotted cords later used by the Inca. Wari shared religious imagery, notably a staff-holding god, with Tiwanaku to the south, and the two powers met but seem to have avoided major war. Around 1000 Wari collapsed, perhaps because of drought and internal unrest, leaving a patchwork of regional states.
empires.legacy: Wari pioneered the roads, administrative centres, terracing and record-keeping that the Inca later built into their own empire.

empires.name: Chimú Empire (Chimor)

peak.note: About 1,000 km of the north Peruvian coast (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Tacaynamo
rulers.note: Founder in Chimú tradition, said to have arrived by sea

rulers.name: Ñançenpinco
rulers.note: Remembered as the conqueror who expanded Chimor

rulers.name: Minchançaman
rulers.note: Last independent king, taken to Cusco by the Inca

empires.summary: The Chimú kingdom, called Chimor, arose around 900 in the Moche valley on Peru's desert north coast, where the Moche civilisation had flourished earlier. Its capital, Chan Chan, was the largest adobe city in the Americas, made up of walled royal compounds, each built by a king who was buried in it with his treasures. Chimú engineers dug long irrigation canals to water the desert, and its craftsmen were skilled goldsmiths and weavers. From the 14th century the Chimú conquered neighbouring valleys until they controlled about 1,000 kilometres of coast, from near the Ecuadorian border to near Lima. Around 1470 the Inca under Topa Inca Yupanqui conquered Chimor, reportedly by cutting its water supply, and carried its king and many artisans off to Cusco.
empires.legacy: Chan Chan is a World Heritage Site, and Chimú metalworkers shaped the gold-working traditions of the Inca court.

empires.name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)

peak.note: From southern Colombia to central Chile; c. 2.0M km² in 1527 (Taagepera 1997; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006)

rulers.name: Manco Cápac
rulers.note: Legendary founder of Cusco

rulers.name: Pachacuti
rulers.note: Began the imperial expansion; rebuilt Cusco

rulers.name: Topa Inca Yupanqui
rulers.note: Conquered Chimor and pushed into Chile

rulers.name: Huayna Capac
rulers.note: Ruled at the empire's height; died in an epidemic, possibly smallpox

rulers.name: Atahualpa
rulers.note: Won the civil war, then was executed by Pizarro

empires.summary: The Inca were a small kingdom around Cusco in the Peruvian highlands, traditionally founded by Manco Cápac around 1200. In 1438 Pachacuti repelled an attack by the rival Chanka and began a series of conquests that his son Topa Inca and grandson Huayna Capac continued, creating Tawantinsuyu, the Land of the Four Quarters, the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas. The Inca ruled some 10 million people through a network of about 40,000 kilometres of roads with rope bridges and relay runners, state storehouses and a labour tax called mit'a, keeping records on knotted khipus. They resettled loyal colonists and spread the Quechua language. A civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa had just ended when Francisco Pizarro arrived; he captured Atahualpa and executed him in 1533.
empires.legacy: Machu Picchu and the Inca roads are world-famous, and Quechua, the Inca state language, is still spoken by millions of Andean people.

sources.title: Taagepera (1997), Expansion and Contraction Patterns of Large Polities
Turchin, Adams & Hall (2006), East-West Orientation of Historical Empires

empires.name: Thule culture
empires.capital: None; small seasonal villages across the Arctic

peak.note: From Alaska across Arctic Canada to Greenland (rough estimate)

rulers.name: No rulers
rulers.note: Thule society was organised in kin-based groups led by experienced whaling captains (umialik)

empires.summary: The Thule people, ancestors of today's Inuit, developed in coastal Alaska around 1000 CE. Using sophisticated technology, including large skin boats called umiaks, kayaks, toggling harpoons, dog sleds and snow houses, they hunted bowhead whales, seals and walrus. From about 1200, perhaps encouraged by warmer conditions and the search for iron and new hunting grounds, they spread rapidly eastward across Arctic Canada to Greenland in just a few generations, replacing the earlier Dorset people. In Greenland they met Norse settlers, whose colonies later vanished. Thule communities were small and mobile, without states or kings, but linked by trade networks stretching thousands of kilometres. As the Little Ice Age cooled the Arctic after about 1400, whaling declined and Thule culture evolved into the regional Inuit cultures met by Europeans.
empires.legacy: The Thule migration created the Inuit world of Alaska, Canada and Greenland, whose inventions such as the kayak are now used worldwide.

sources.title: Historical Climatology: What made the Thule move? (on Friesen & Arnold 2008)

empires.name: Tuʻi Tonga Empire
empires.capital: Toloa and Heketā, then Muʻa, all on Tongatapu

peak.note: Rough upper bound counting the land of Tonga, Samoa, ʻUvea, Futuna and Fiji; Tonga itself has about 750 km² of land, and its maritime influence spread far wider

rulers.name: ʻAhoʻeitu
rulers.note: First Tuʻi Tonga, said to be the son of the god Tangaloa

rulers.name: Tuʻitātui
rulers.note: Credited with building the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon

rulers.name: Takalaua

rulers.name: Laufilitonga
rulers.note: Last Tuʻi Tonga

empires.summary: According to Tongan tradition, the line of sacred kings called Tuʻi Tonga began around 950 with ʻAhoʻeitu, son of the sky god Tangaloa and a mortal woman. From Tongatapu, the Tuʻi Tonga built a maritime chiefdom whose influence, through voyaging canoes, marriage alliances and tribute, extended at its height in the 12th and 13th centuries across Samoa, ʻUvea (Wallis), Futuna and parts of Fiji. The royal centre at Muʻa has great stone-faced tombs called langi, and the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon is attributed to the king Tuʻitātui. After several Tuʻi Tonga were assassinated, around the 15th century they handed political power to a new line, the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, and later the Tuʻi Kanokupolu, keeping a sacred role. The title lapsed when Laufilitonga died in 1865, as George Tupou I unified Tonga as a modern kingdom.
empires.legacy: The Tuʻi Tonga tradition underpins the modern Kingdom of Tonga, the only Pacific island monarchy never formally colonised.

empires.name: Spanish Empire

(Alliance between Papal States and Spanish Empire)
empires.capital: Madrid from 1561 (Valladolid 1601–1606); earlier the court moved between Toledo, Valladolid and other cities

peak.note: c. 13.7M km² (Taagepera 1997), including vast claimed but thinly settled lands in North and South America, plus the Philippines; c. 13.7M km² (Taagepera 1997)

rulers.name: Isabella I and Ferdinand II

rulers.name: Alfonso XIII

rulers.name: Francisco Franco

empires.summary: Spain's empire grew from the union of Castile and Aragon under Isabella and Ferdinand, who in 1492 conquered Granada and sponsored Columbus's first voyage. Within two generations conquistadors toppled the Aztec and Inca empires, and silver from Potosí and Zacatecas paid for Habsburg wars across Europe, where Charles V and Philip II also ruled the Netherlands, much of Italy and, from 1580 to 1640, Portugal. The Americas were run through viceroyalties, royal courts and the Catholic Church, with Indigenous labour forced through the encomienda and mita systems and enslaved Africans shipped in. After Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808, the mainland American colonies won independence by 1825. Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines were lost to the United States in 1898, and the last African holdings were given up by 1976.
empires.legacy: Spanish is now the first language of nearly 500 million people, and Catholic churches, grid-plan towns and legal traditions across the Americas and the Philippines trace back to Spanish rule.

empires.name: Portuguese Empire

peak.note: Nominal extent, mostly Brazil, shortly before its independence in 1822 (10.4M km², Brzezinski 2012); Taagepera (1997), counting only effectively controlled land, gives c. 5.5M km² for 1820

rulers.name: John I
rulers.note: Captured Ceuta in 1415; father of Prince Henry the Navigator

rulers.name: Manuel I
rulers.note: Vasco da Gama reached India and Cabral reached Brazil in his reign

rulers.name: John III
rulers.note: Began the colonisation of Brazil; trade reached Japan

rulers.name: John IV

rulers.name: John VI
rulers.note: Ruled the empire from Rio de Janeiro after fleeing Napoleon

rulers.name: António de Oliveira Salazar
rulers.note: Dictator who fought to keep the African colonies

empires.summary: Portugal, a small Atlantic kingdom, began Europe's age of overseas empire when it captured Ceuta in Morocco in 1415. Encouraged by Prince Henry the Navigator, its sailors crept down the African coast until Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Rather than conquering large lands, Portugal first built a chain of fortified trading posts from Elmina and Mozambique to Goa, Malacca and Macau, controlling the spice trade with naval power. Brazil, claimed in 1500, became the heart of the empire through sugar, gold and the labour of millions of enslaved Africans. The royal court fled to Rio de Janeiro in 1808, and Brazil became independent in 1822. Portugal clung to Angola, Mozambique and Guinea until a revolution at home in 1974 ended long colonial wars; Macau was returned to China in 1999.
empires.legacy: Portuguese is spoken by some 250 million people on four continents, and the empire's Atlantic slave trade reshaped the populations of Brazil and Africa.

empires.name: British Empire
aliases: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

peak.note: c. 35.5M km² (Taagepera 1997); about a quarter of the world's land and a quarter of its people

rulers.name: Elizabeth I
rulers.note: Her reign saw the first English colonial ventures and the East India Company's charter

rulers.name: George III
rulers.note: Won Canada and India from France but lost the American colonies

rulers.name: Victoria
rulers.note: Empress of India from 1876

rulers.name: George V
rulers.note: Reigned as the empire reached its greatest size

rulers.name: Winston Churchill
rulers.note: Prime minister who led the empire through the Second World War

rulers.name: Elizabeth II
rulers.note: Oversaw decolonisation and the modern Commonwealth

empires.summary: England's overseas expansion began with Atlantic claims and colonies in Virginia, New England and the Caribbean, built by chartered companies, sugar plantations and the slave trade. After union with Scotland in 1707, Britain beat France for North America and India in the Seven Years' War, then lost thirteen colonies in the American Revolution. It rebuilt in Asia, Africa and the Pacific: the East India Company conquered India, convicts and settlers founded Australia, and in the scramble for Africa Britain took Egypt, Nigeria, Kenya and lands from the Cape towards Cairo. Rule ranged from self-governing settler dominions to direct rule and indirect rule through princes and chiefs, all guarded by the Royal Navy. Two world wars drained its strength; India's independence in 1947 began rapid decolonisation, and Hong Kong's return to China in 1997 is often taken as the end.
empires.legacy: English became a global language, and parliamentary government, common law and railways spread with the empire, as did lasting scars from conquest, famine and partition. Most former colonies remain linked through the Commonwealth.

empires.name: French Colonial Empire
clio: French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon

peak.note: c. 11.5M km² (Taagepera 1997); most of it in North, West and Central Africa

rulers.name: Louis XIV
rulers.note: His minister Colbert built up New France, the Caribbean colonies and overseas trade

rulers.name: Louis XV
rulers.note: Lost Canada and most of India to Britain in 1763

rulers.name: Napoleon I
rulers.note: Failed to restore slavery in Saint-Domingue and sold Louisiana in 1803

rulers.name: Napoleon III
rulers.note: Expanded into Senegal, Indochina and New Caledonia

rulers.name: Jules Ferry
rulers.note: Prime minister who drove expansion into Tunisia, Indochina and Africa

rulers.name: Charles de Gaulle
rulers.note: President who ended the Algerian War and granted African independence

empires.summary: France's first colonial empire began with Jacques Cartier's voyages to the St Lawrence in 1534 and grew into New France, a vast fur-trading realm reaching down the Mississippi to Louisiana, plus rich sugar islands such as Saint-Domingue worked by enslaved Africans. Defeat by Britain in 1763 cost Canada and most of India, the Haitian Revolution freed Saint-Domingue, and Napoleon sold Louisiana in 1803. A second empire began with the invasion of Algeria in 1830 and spread across West and Equatorial Africa, Madagascar, Indochina and, after 1919, Syria and Lebanon. Paris governed centrally, claiming a civilising mission and assimilating a small educated elite. After the Second World War, defeat in Vietnam in 1954 and a brutal war in Algeria, independent in 1962, brought most colonies to independence; some islands remain parts of France today.
empires.legacy: French is still widely spoken across West and Central Africa, and overseas departments such as Martinique, Guadeloupe and Réunion remain part of France.

empires.name: Dutch Republic and Dutch Colonial Empire
clio: Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands
empires.capital: Amsterdam (government at The Hague); Batavia in the East Indies

peak.note: c. 2.1M km² (Oxford figure cited in Wikipedia's list; not covered by Taagepera); mostly the Netherlands Indies, today's Indonesia, plus Suriname

rulers.name: William the Silent
rulers.note: Prince of Orange who led the revolt against Spain

rulers.name: Maurice of Nassau

rulers.name: Johan de Witt

empires.summary: The Dutch Republic was born when seven northern provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands revolted against Philip II of Spain and renounced his rule in 1581. Its merchants built the most advanced commercial economy of the 17th century, and two chartered firms, the Dutch East India Company (VOC, 1602) and the West India Company (1621), carved out an empire of trade. The VOC seized the Spice Islands from Portugal, founded Batavia (Jakarta) in 1619 and held Ceylon, the Cape and a post at Nagasaki, while the West India Company briefly held northeastern Brazil and New Amsterdam, later New York. After the VOC collapsed in 1799, the Netherlands, a kingdom from 1815, ruled the East Indies directly and forced farmers to grow export crops. Indonesia won independence in 1949 after a war, and Suriname left in 1975.
empires.legacy: Afrikaans, Dutch place names from New York to South Africa, and modern financial tools such as the stock exchange all trace back to the Dutch golden age.

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Dutch East India Company

empires.name: Belgium and the Belgian Congo

peak.note: c. 2.43M km² (Wikipedia); the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi were about 80 times the size of Belgium

empires.summary: Belgium broke away from the Netherlands in 1830 and became a constitutional kingdom under Leopold I. His son Leopold II, eager for a colony, used explorers and a front of humanitarian societies to win international recognition at the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 for the Congo Free State, which he owned personally. Its rubber and ivory profits were extracted through forced labour, hostage-taking and mutilation, and millions died from violence, famine and disease. International outrage forced Belgium to annex the territory as the Belgian Congo in 1908. The state, the Catholic Church and mining companies then ran it as a paternalist colony that allowed Africans almost no higher education. After the First World War Belgium also governed Ruanda-Urundi. Congo became independent in 1960, and Rwanda and Burundi in 1962.
empires.legacy: The Congo Free State became a worldwide symbol of colonial atrocity, and its exploitation shaped the troubled history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

empires.name: Habsburg Monarchy (Austrian Empire, Austria-Hungary)

peak.note: c.; Austria-Hungary was c. 622,000 km² in 1905 (Encyclopaedia Britannica 1911), plus Bosnia-Herzegovina (c. 51,000 km²), annexed in 1908

rulers.note: Gained Bohemia and Hungary after Mohács; Holy Roman Emperor from 1556

rulers.name: Leopold I

empires.summary: The Austrian Habsburgs, Holy Roman Emperors almost continuously since 1438, became a great power when Archduke Ferdinand I inherited the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary after the Battle of Mohács in 1526. Their multinational realm, ruled from Vienna, held off the Ottomans at the sieges of 1529 and 1683 and then reconquered Hungary. Maria Theresa and her son Joseph II reformed the army, taxes and schools, while wars with Prussia cost them Silesia. Francis I declared an Austrian Empire in 1804 and dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Defeat by Prussia in 1866 led to the Compromise of 1867, creating Austria-Hungary, a dual monarchy of two governments under one emperor. Rising nationalism among Czechs, Poles, Serbs and others strained it, and after defeat in the First World War it broke apart in 1918.
empires.legacy: Vienna's music and architecture flowered under the Habsburgs, and the successor states of Central Europe, from Czechoslovakia to Yugoslavia, were drawn from the empire's ruins.

empires.name: Tsardom of Russia and Russian Empire

peak.note: c. 22.8M km² (Taagepera 1997; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006), after the conquest of Central Asia; Alaska had been sold in 1867

rulers.name: Nicholas II

empires.summary: Moscow's grand princes threw off Mongol overlordship and gathered the Russian lands, and in 1547 Ivan IV, the Terrible, was crowned the first Tsar of All Russia. His conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan opened the Volga, and Cossacks and fur traders crossed Siberia to reach the Pacific by 1639. After the chaotic Time of Troubles, the Romanov dynasty took power in 1613. Peter the Great built a modern army and navy, founded St Petersburg and proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721; Catherine the Great added Crimea, the Black Sea steppe and much of Poland. In the 19th century Russia took Finland, the Caucasus and Central Asia. The tsars ruled as autocrats over a peasant majority, most of them serfs until 1861. Defeats and hardship in the First World War led to revolution in 1917 and the end of the monarchy.
empires.legacy: Russia became the largest country on Earth, and the expansion that brought dozens of peoples under Moscow's rule still shapes politics from the Baltic to the Pacific.

empires.name: Soviet Union (USSR)

peak.note: About one-sixth of the world's land surface; official area 22.4M km²; Taagepera (1997) gives c. 22.3M km² for 1945

rulers.name: Joseph Stalin
rulers.note: Dictator of forced collectivisation, purges and victory over Nazi Germany

rulers.name: Nikita Khrushchev
rulers.note: Denounced Stalin; Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962

rulers.name: Leonid Brezhnev
rulers.note: Era of stability and later stagnation

rulers.name: Mikhail Gorbachev
rulers.note: His reforms, glasnost and perestroika, preceded the union's collapse

empires.summary: The Soviet Union grew out of the October Revolution of 1917, when Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd and then won a brutal civil war. In 1922 Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the Transcaucasian republics formed the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, a one-party state run by the Communist Party from Moscow. Under Stalin it forced peasants into collective farms, industrialised at terrible human cost and sent millions to Gulag labour camps. Invaded by Nazi Germany in 1941, it lost around 27 million people but drove on to Berlin, then dominated Eastern Europe through allied communist regimes. It rivalled the United States in the Cold War, launching the first satellite and the first human into space. Economic stagnation, Gorbachev's reforms and nationalist movements led to its breakup into fifteen independent states in December 1991.
empires.legacy: The Cold War rivalry it led divided the world for four decades, and Russian remains a common language across its fifteen successor states.

empires.name: Russian Federation

peak.note: The largest country on Earth; c. 17.1M km² (Taagepera 1997)

rulers.name: Boris Yeltsin
rulers.note: First president; led the shift to a market economy

rulers.name: Vladimir Putin
rulers.note: Recentralised power; prime minister 2008–2012

rulers.name: Dmitry Medvedev
