empires.summary: Māori settled New Zealand around 1300, making it one of the last major land masses to be peopled. British colonisation began in earnest after the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, signed by representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs, though its English and Māori versions differed on sovereignty. Disputes over land led to the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s to 1870s and large confiscations of Māori land. Settlers built a farming economy exporting wool, meat and butter to Britain. New Zealand became a self-governing colony and, in 1893, the first country to give women the vote in national elections. It became a dominion in 1907 and fought for Britain in both world wars. Full independence was adopted in 1947, and from the 1970s the country revived Māori rights and adopted a nuclear-free policy.
empires.legacy: New Zealand is known for pioneering social reforms, and te reo Māori is an official language alongside English and New Zealand Sign Language.

moments.title: Farming begins
moments.place: Jericho and the Fertile Crescent (southern Levant)
moments.summary: In the Fertile Crescent, people began cultivating wild cereals such as barley around 9500 BCE and settled in permanent villages like Jericho, founded beside a spring between about 9500 and 9000 BCE. Over the following one to two thousand years emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas, bitter vetch and flax became fully domesticated crops, and the region's wild sheep, goats, cattle and pigs became farm animals.
moments.why: Farming fed far more people from the same land than hunting and gathering, making possible permanent villages, food surpluses, growing populations and, in time, towns, specialists and states.
moments.also: Farming was invented independently in several other places: rice and millet in China (rice domesticated between about 13,500 and 8,200 years ago), taro and yams at Kuk in New Guinea (perhaps from 8000 BCE), squash and maize in Mesoamerica (maize from about 7000 BCE), potatoes and manioc in South America, sorghum and pearl millet in Africa, and sunflowers and other seed plants in eastern North America (c. 2500 BCE).

moments.title: Çatalhöyük, an early proto-city
moments.summary: On the Konya plain of Anatolia, farmers built a tightly packed settlement of mudbrick houses with no streets: people walked across the rooftops and climbed down into their homes by ladder. Houses were plastered and decorated with wall paintings and bull horns, and the dead were buried beneath the floors. Older estimates put its population at 5,000 or more; recent excavations suggest perhaps 600–800 people in a typical year of its middle phase.
moments.why: Çatalhöyük shows early farmers living together in large numbers for some 2,000 years without palaces, temples or obvious rulers, making it a key site for understanding the step from village life towards towns.

moments.title: Copper smelting begins
moments.place: Belovode, near Petrovac na Mlavi (eastern Serbia)
moments.summary: At Belovode, a village of the Vinča culture in the Balkans, copper slag dated to about 5000 BCE is the oldest securely dated evidence of smelting copper from ore at high temperature. Within a few centuries metal was spreading across south-eastern Europe: the cemetery at Varna on the Black Sea coast (c. 4600–4300 BCE) held copper tools and some 3,000 gold objects, often called the oldest gold treasure in the world.
moments.why: Smelting turned rock into tools, ornaments and portable wealth, opening the Copper Age, and rich graves like those at Varna show metal sharpening the divide between elites and everyone else.
moments.also: Early copper-working is also documented in the Near East, and around the North American Great Lakes people of the Old Copper complex cold-hammered native copper from about 6500 BCE, though without smelting it.

sources.title: Radivojević, Archaeometallurgy of the Vinča culture: Belovode in eastern Serbia (Historical Metallurgy 47)

moments.title: The wheel and the plough
moments.summary: Wheeled vehicles appear almost at once across a wide area in the second half of the 4th millennium BCE: a pot from Bronocice in Poland (c. 3600–3400 BCE) is incised with a four-wheeled wagon, pictographs from Uruk show wagons around 3500–3350 BCE, and the oldest surviving wooden wheel, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, dates to about 3340–3030 BCE. In the same era farmers in the Near East harnessed oxen to the ard, a simple scratch plough, part of a wider shift to using animals for pulling, milk and wool.
moments.why: Animal power multiplied the land a farming family could work and the loads it could move, opening up new land and making heavy overland transport practical.
moments.also: In Mesoamerica the wheel was invented independently but was used only on small wheeled toys, never for transport before the 16th century.

moments.title: Writing is invented
moments.summary: In the temple district of Uruk, scribes began pressing signs into clay tablets around 3300 BCE to keep accounts of grain, animals and labour, a system that grew out of older clay accounting tokens. This proto-cuneiform developed into cuneiform, used for Sumerian, Akkadian and many other languages for some 3,000 years. In Egypt, labels from tomb U-j at Abydos (c. 3400–3200 BCE) show the beginnings of hieroglyphs, usually counted as a separate invention.
moments.why: Writing let people store information beyond human memory, run large states and economies, and record laws, letters and literature; it marks the line between prehistory and history.
moments.also: Writing was invented independently at least twice more: in Shang China (oracle-bone inscriptions, c. 1250 BCE) and in Mesoamerica, where Maya inscriptions date from the 3rd century BCE and possible earlier Olmec writing is debated.

moments.title: Uruk, the first great city
moments.summary: In the Late Uruk period, Uruk grew to some 250 hectares and perhaps 25,000–50,000 people, with tens of thousands more in its surrounding territory, the largest urban area in the world at the time. Its walled Eanna temple district had monumental temples, administrators using cylinder seals and tablets, and mass-produced ration bowls, and Uruk-style outposts spread from western Iran to south-eastern Anatolia.
moments.why: Uruk is the earliest clear example of a city-state, with social classes, full-time specialists, temples and bureaucrats, a pattern of urban life soon repeated across Mesopotamia.

moments.title: Egypt is unified
moments.summary: Kings from Upper (southern) Egypt took control of the Nile Delta, completing a unification begun by earlier rulers. The Narmer Palette, found at Nekhen, shows King Narmer, usually identified with the legendary Menes, wearing the crowns of both Upper and Lower Egypt. The First Dynasty ruled from Memphis, where the Nile valley meets the delta.
moments.why: Unification created a single kingdom along the Nile under one king, with writing and a bureaucracy, and pharaonic rule endured, with interruptions, for about 3,000 years.

moments.title: Bronze comes into wide use
moments.place: Anatolia and Mesopotamia (Kestel tin mine, southern Türkiye)
moments.summary: Metalworkers found that adding arsenic or, better, tin to copper made a harder alloy, bronze. Arsenical bronze came first (the Maykop culture of the North Caucasus used it by the mid-4th millennium BCE), and by about 3000 BCE the Bronze Age had begun across much of the Old World, from Mesopotamia and Egypt to the Indus. Because tin is rare, bronze depended on long-distance trade; Kestel in southern Türkiye was mined for tin from about 3250 BCE.
moments.why: Bronze tools and weapons were tougher than copper ones, and the hunt for tin and copper tied distant regions together in the first long-distance metal trade networks.
moments.also: A tin-bronze foil from Pločnik in Serbia may date to c. 4650 BCE, though its dating is disputed. In China bronze-working took hold later, with early centres in the north-west by c. 2500–2300 BCE and large-scale casting at Erlitou.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tin sources and trade in ancient times

moments.title: Caral, first cities of the Americas
moments.summary: On Peru's dry north-central coast, the Caral–Supe (Norte Chico) civilisation built the earliest known monumental centres in the Americas, with large-scale construction from about 3200 BCE. Caral itself, inhabited from about 2600 to 2000 BCE, had six monumental complexes each built around a pyramid, sunken circular plazas and around 3,000 residents. Its people irrigated cotton for fishing nets and textiles, ate fish and shellfish as well as crops, and made no pottery.
moments.why: Caral shows that cities and monumental architecture arose in the Americas entirely independently, and almost as early as in Egypt and Mesopotamia.

moments.title: Indus Valley cities flourish
moments.summary: In its mature phase the Indus civilisation built planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, each with perhaps 30,000–60,000 people, laid out on grids with baked-brick houses and covered street drains. Spread over more than 1,000 settlements from Afghanistan and Balochistan to Gujarat, it covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, yet no clear palaces or temples have been found and its script is still undeciphered.
moments.why: The Indus cities were among the world's first urban societies, with some of the earliest known city sanitation, and show that early urban life could flourish without obvious palaces or royal monuments.

moments.title: The Great Pyramid rises
moments.summary: For the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khufu, Egyptians built the Great Pyramid at Giza, originally about 146.6 m tall, over roughly 26 years. Excavated workers' camps point to organised, conscripted labour rather than slaves, perhaps 13,000 on average and up to about 40,000 at peak, and the papyrus diary of an official named Merer records limestone being shipped to the site in Khufu's 27th year.
moments.why: It was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,700 years and shows how far an early state could organise labour, food supply and engineering.

moments.title: Sargon builds the first empire
moments.summary: Sargon, who in later legend began as cupbearer to the king of Kish, defeated Lugal-zage-si of Uruk around 2300 BCE, took control of Sumer to the Persian Gulf, and campaigned from Elam in Iran to Mari and Syria. He ruled from Akkad, a city whose site has never been found, and at its height around 2250 BCE his dynasty's empire reached from the Mediterranean to Iran.
moments.why: Often called the world's first empire (historians debate the label), Akkad set the pattern of one king ruling many conquered cities and peoples, with a professional army and Akkadian as a shared language of government.

moments.title: Horses and war chariots
moments.summary: Ancient DNA shows that the ancestors of nearly all modern domestic horses were domesticated around 2200 BCE in the Volga–Don region of the western Eurasian steppe. Soon after, people of the Sintashta culture east of the Urals, who built fortified settlements such as Arkaim, buried light chariots with spoked wheels, the oldest known, in graves dated to around 2000 BCE, often together with these horses.
moments.why: Fast horses and chariots transformed warfare, travel and communication: within about 500 years chariots appeared in Greece, Egypt and Mesopotamia, and they reached Shang China around 1200 BCE.

moments.title: Code of Hammurabi
moments.summary: Late in his reign (c. 1792–1750 BCE), King Hammurabi of Babylon had about 282 laws carved on a 2.25 m basalt stele crowned by an image of the sun god Shamash. The laws cover trade, wages, family and property, set penalties that differed by social class, and include the principle of an eye for an eye. Centuries later the stele was carried off to Susa in Iran as plunder; it was found there in 1901 and is now in the Louvre.
moments.why: It is the best-known early law collection, a ruler's public statement of fixed rules for justice, and it made the idea of written, displayed law famous across the ages.
moments.also: It was not the first: the earlier Mesopotamian law collections of Ur-Nammu, Lipit-Ishtar and Eshnunna are known.

sources.title: Louvre: Law Code of Hammurabi, King of Babylon

moments.title: The Vedas are composed
moments.summary: In the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, poets composed the Rigveda, 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, most likely between about 1500 and 1000 BCE, and it was gathered into a fixed collection around 1200–1000 BCE. Passed down orally with remarkable precision for many centuries before being written down, it was followed by the other Vedas and, from roughly the 7th–6th centuries BCE (dates are debated), by the philosophical Upanishads.
moments.why: The Vedas are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, and the Upanishads' ideas of brahman, atman and karma became central to Indian religion and philosophy.

moments.title: Shang bronzes and oracle bones
moments.summary: At Yin, the last capital of the Shang dynasty near modern Anyang, kings consulted their ancestors by cracking turtle shells and ox shoulder blades with heat and carving the questions and answers onto them. These oracle-bone inscriptions, beginning in the reign of Wu Ding around 1250 BCE, are the earliest substantial body of Chinese writing, with around 5,000 different characters. The same court cast magnificent bronze ritual vessels, like those in the tomb of Fu Hao, Wu Ding's consort and a war leader.
moments.why: The oracle-bone script is the ancestor of the Chinese characters still in use today, making Chinese one of the world's longest continuously used writing systems.

moments.title: Olmec civilisation flourishes
moments.summary: In the tropical lowlands of Mexico's Gulf Coast, the Olmecs built San Lorenzo, the largest city in Mesoamerica from about 1200 to 900 BCE, before La Venta became their leading centre (c. 900–400 BCE). They carved colossal stone heads up to about 3 m tall and weighing many tonnes, probably portraits of rulers, and buried rich offerings of jade and serpentine.
moments.why: Often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica (a debated label), the Olmecs pioneered monumental art and possibly ideas such as the ballgame and the Long Count calendar that shaped later civilisations like the Maya.

moments.title: Late Bronze Age collapse
moments.summary: Within a few decades around 1200 BCE, the interconnected palace kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart. The Hittite Empire broke up, the Mycenaean palaces of Greece were abandoned, and the port of Ugarit was destroyed around 1190–1185 BCE, its last letters warning of enemy ships; Egypt and Assyria survived but were weakened. Recent studies suggest fewer cities were destroyed than once believed.
moments.why: The collapse ended an age of palace-run kingdoms and long-distance trade and cleared the way for the Iron Age world of new peoples, iron tools and the alphabet; its causes probably combined drought, earthquakes, migrations including the Sea Peoples, and fragile, over-centralised states.

moments.title: Iron working spreads
moments.summary: Iron had long been known in small amounts, from meteorites and occasional smelting, but around 1300–1200 BCE smiths in Anatolia and neighbouring regions mastered smelting iron ore, which needs far higher temperatures than bronze. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE ironworking spread across the eastern Mediterranean, and smiths learned to harden iron into steel by heating it in charcoal and quenching it. The old idea that the Hittites guarded the secret of iron is no longer accepted.
moments.why: Iron ore is far more common than tin, so once smelting was mastered, iron tools and weapons became cheap and widespread, transforming farming and warfare.
moments.also: Iron was worked early, and probably independently, elsewhere: in India's Ganges plain from about 1800–1200 BCE, in sub-Saharan Africa (see Nok), and in China, which was making cast iron by the 5th century BCE.

moments.title: The Phoenician alphabet
moments.summary: Phoenician scribes in coastal cities such as Byblos used a script of just 22 letters, each standing for a consonant, developed from the earlier Proto-Sinaitic script, which was itself derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs. Its conventional starting date is c. 1050 BCE, and the inscription on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos, usually dated to around 1000 BCE, is the earliest known example of the fully developed alphabet.
moments.why: Carried by Phoenician traders around the Mediterranean, it became the ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets and, through Aramaic, of the Hebrew and Arabic scripts; a couple of dozen letters made reading and writing far easier to learn than systems with hundreds of signs.
moments.also: At Ugarit, scribes had earlier used a 30-letter alphabet written in cuneiform wedges (c. 1400 BCE), whose letter order resembles the Phoenician.

moments.title: Lapita voyagers reach Polynesia
moments.summary: The Lapita people, Austronesian-speaking seafarers known for their pottery decorated with toothed stamps, had settled the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea by about 1600–1200 BCE. After 1200 BCE they sailed east into previously uninhabited islands, reaching Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and high-precision dating puts their founding settlement at Nukuleka in Tonga, the first landfall in Polynesia, at about 890 BCE.
moments.why: Crossing hundreds of kilometres of open ocean in outrigger canoes, the Lapita began the human settlement of Remote Oceania, which their Polynesian descendants would later carry across the Pacific.

sources.title: Burley, Weisler & Zhao (2012), High Precision U/Th Dating of First Polynesian Settlement, PLoS ONE

moments.title: First Olympic Games
moments.summary: According to tradition, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BCE at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia, with a single footrace, the stadion, won by Koroibos of Elis; archaeology suggests major games began nearer 700 BCE. Held every four years for free-born Greek men, the games were protected by a sacred truce for travellers and continued until the late 4th century CE or a little later.
moments.why: The four-year Olympiad became a common Greek way of dating events, the games gave rival Greek city-states a shared festival and identity, and they inspired the modern Olympic Games.

moments.title: Iron smelting in West Africa
moments.summary: The Nok culture of central Nigeria, famous for its hollow, near life-sized terracotta sculptures, was smelting iron in bloomery furnaces by about 550 BCE and perhaps from 750 BCE or earlier. Excavations at Taruga uncovered iron slag, clay furnace pipes and wrought iron, helping to show that the Nok people lived in an Iron Age.
moments.why: Early dates at Nok and other sites match or predate known ironworking at Carthage and Meroë, so many archaeologists now argue that iron smelting was invented independently south of the Sahara, though the evidence is still debated.
moments.also: Even earlier smelting dates claimed for sites in Niger (Termit, c. 1500 BCE) and Nigeria (Lejja) remain disputed.

moments.title: First coins in Lydia
moments.summary: In Lydia and the neighbouring Greek cities of Ionia, the first coins, small lumps of electrum (a natural gold–silver alloy) stamped with a design, were struck in the late 7th century BCE; the electrum coin of Phanes from Ephesus dates to about 625–600 BCE. Around 550 BCE King Croesus issued the first coins of refined gold and silver, and workshops for separating electrum into pure gold and silver have been excavated at the Lydian capital, Sardis.
moments.why: Coins of guaranteed weight and purity made trade, taxes and paying soldiers far simpler, and coinage soon spread through the Greek and Persian worlds.
moments.also: In China, shovel-shaped bronze coins were cast at a mint in Henan between about 640 and 550 BCE, a separate tradition; India's punch-marked coins followed by the 4th century BCE, possibly earlier.

moments.title: Cyrus founds the Persian Empire
moments.summary: Cyrus II, king of Anshan in Persis, overthrew his Median overlord Astyages around 550 BCE and built his capital, Pasargadae, near the site of his victory. He went on to conquer Lydia (546 BCE) and Babylon (539 BCE), where the Cyrus Cylinder presents him as a restorer of temples and of displaced peoples; the Bible credits him with letting exiled Jews return to Jerusalem.
moments.why: By his death in 530 BCE the Achaemenid Persian Empire stretched from Asia Minor to the Indus, the largest empire the world had yet seen, uniting many peoples, languages and religions under one king.

moments.title: Democracy in Athens
moments.summary: The reformer Cleisthenes reorganised the citizens of Athens into ten tribes based on where they lived rather than on family, created a Council of 500 chosen by lot, and strengthened the Assembly, where any adult male citizen could speak and vote. He called the system isonomia, equality before the law.
moments.why: Athens became the best-known early democracy, where ordinary citizens debated and decided policy directly, though women, slaves and foreign residents were excluded, so voters were a minority of adults.

moments.title: The Axial Age thinkers
moments.place: Bodh Gaya (Bihar, India) and across Eurasia
moments.summary: Within a few centuries, thinkers across Eurasia laid the foundations of lasting religions and philosophies: the Buddha (enlightened at Bodh Gaya; his dates are debated, c. 563–483 or c. 480–400 BCE) and Mahavira in India, Confucius (traditionally 551–479 BCE) and, according to tradition, Laozi in China, the Hebrew prophets in Israel, and Greek philosophers from Heraclitus and Parmenides to Plato. In 1949 the philosopher Karl Jaspers named this period, roughly the 8th to 3rd centuries BCE, the Axial Age.
moments.why: Buddhism, Jainism, Confucianism, Daoism, the prophetic tradition of Judaism and Greek philosophy still shape the ethics and beliefs of billions of people; scholars debate whether this was one connected shift or a convenient label for separate developments.

moments.title: The Persian Wars
moments.summary: After Athens helped the Ionian Greeks revolt against Persia, King Darius sent an expedition that the Athenians and Plataeans defeated at Marathon in 490 BCE. In 480 BCE Xerxes invaded with a far larger force, won at Thermopylae and sacked an evacuated Athens, but lost the sea battle of Salamis; Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE ended the invasion.
moments.why: Greek independence survived, Athens rose as a naval power at the head of the Delian League, and its classical age followed; Herodotus' account of the wars earned him the title Father of History.

moments.title: Alexander's conquests
moments.summary: Alexander III of Macedon crossed into Asia in 334 BCE, beat the Persians at the Granicus, Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331), took Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, and overthrew the Achaemenid Empire. He pushed on to the Indus, defeating King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, until his army refused to go further; he died at Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32.
moments.why: His conquests and the kingdoms of his successors spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to north-western India, opening the Hellenistic age in which Greek became a shared language across the region and cultures mixed, from Greco-Buddhist art to Alexandrian science.

moments.title: Euclid and the Library of Alexandria
moments.summary: In Alexandria, Ptolemy I founded the Mouseion, a research institute whose great library, probably established under Ptolemy II (r. 285–246 BCE), gathered somewhere between tens and hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Working in the city around 300 BCE, Euclid wrote the Elements, 13 books that build geometry and number theory step by step from definitions and postulates; later scholars there included Eratosthenes, who calculated the Earth's circumference.
moments.why: The Elements was the core of mathematics teaching for some 2,000 years and has appeared in more than 1,000 printed editions, while the library became a lasting symbol of the ambition to collect all knowledge in one place.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews): Euclid

moments.title: Ashoka turns from war
moments.summary: In about the eighth year of his reign, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga on India's east coast; his own Rock Edict 13 records 100,000 killed and 150,000 carried off, and expresses deep remorse. He turned to dhamma, a moral code of non-violence and right conduct not tied to a single religion, proclaimed it in edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, and became a lay follower and patron of Buddhism.
moments.why: Ashoka is remembered as a ruler who renounced conquest by war, and the missionaries he is credited with sending, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka, helped Buddhism spread beyond India.

moments.title: Qin unifies China
moments.summary: After conquering the last of the rival Warring States, King Ying Zheng of Qin proclaimed himself Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor, in 221 BCE. He replaced hereditary lords with appointed officials in 36 commanderies and standardised the script, coins, weights, measures and even cart axle widths, while linking northern walls, building roads and ordering the burning of books from rival schools of thought.
moments.why: Although the Qin dynasty fell in 206 BCE, after only 15 years, it created the centralised imperial system and common written script that held China together under emperors until 1911.

moments.title: The Han dynasty begins
moments.summary: Liu Bang, born into a peasant family, rose from minor Qin official to rebel leader, defeated his rival Xiang Yu at Gaixia and became emperor in 202 BCE, remembered as Emperor Gaozu of Han. Keeping much of the Qin's centralised system but easing its harsh laws and taxes, the Han ruled from Chang'an and, after a brief break (9–23 CE), from Luoyang until 220 CE.
moments.why: Under the Han, Confucianism became the state ideology and a census of 2 CE counted some 57.7 million people; the dynasty became so central to Chinese identity that China's majority still call themselves the Han people and their writing Han characters.

moments.title: Paper is invented in China
moments.summary: The oldest surviving fragment of paper, apparently part of a map, was found at Fangmatan in Gansu and dates to about 179–141 BCE. Early paper made from plant fibres was used mostly for wrapping and padding, for example around bronze mirrors, and only later for writing. In 105 CE the court official Cai Lun refined papermaking using bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets, which is why he was long credited with inventing it.
moments.why: Cheap, light paper gradually replaced bamboo, silk and parchment, reaching the Islamic world and then Europe by the 11th century, and made books and records far more widely available.

moments.title: Rome destroys Carthage and Corinth
moments.summary: In early 146 BCE, after a three-year siege in the Third Punic War, Roman troops under Scipio Aemilianus stormed Carthage, destroyed the city and sold some 50,000 survivors into slavery; its lands became the Roman province of Africa. In the same year Lucius Mummius defeated the Achaean League and sacked Corinth, bringing mainland Greece under direct Roman control.
moments.why: With its great rival gone and Greece subdued, Rome became the unchallenged power of the Mediterranean, and the flood of Greek art and learning into Rome reshaped Roman culture.

moments.title: The Silk Road opens
moments.summary: Around 138 BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent the envoy Zhang Qian west to seek allies against the Xiongnu. After years as a Xiongnu captive he reached Dayuan (Ferghana), the Yuezhi and Bactria, and returned to Chang'an in 125 BCE with reports of rich states to the west. Han embassies, campaigns and trade followed, and by around 114 BCE a network of routes linked China with Central Asia and, in time, the Roman world.
moments.why: For some 1,500 years the Silk Road carried silk, horses, paper and ideas across more than 6,400 km of Eurasia, linking civilisations that had known little of one another.

moments.title: From Caesar to Augustus
moments.summary: On 15 March 44 BCE, about 60 senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Julius Caesar, recently named dictator for life, in the Curia of Pompey in Rome. His heir Octavian joined Mark Antony and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, then defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE; in 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus.
moments.why: Augustus became Rome's first emperor, ending the Republic and founding the Principate, a system of one-man rule behind republican forms that opened a long era of relative peace known as the Pax Romana.

moments.title: Birth of Jesus
moments.summary: Jesus of Nazareth was probably born between about 6 and 4 BCE, since the Gospels place his birth in the reign of King Herod, whose death is usually dated to 4 BCE. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke set his birth in Bethlehem, though many historians think he was more likely born in Nazareth in Galilee, where he grew up.
moments.why: Christianity, which grew from his life and teachings, became one of the world's largest religions, and the Anno Domini year count devised by Dionysius Exiguus in 525 CE, which placed his birth a few years too late, underlies today's common calendar era.

journeys.name: Sumerian city-states
journeys.summary: In the marshy south of Mesopotamia, Uruk and its neighbours grew into the world's first cities and, by c. 3300 BCE, the first writing. Through the Early Dynastic period (c. 2900–2334 BCE) rival city-states such as Kish, Ur, Lagash and Umma fought over land and water, until Lugalzagesi united Sumer, only to lose it to Sargon of Akkad. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).

events.text: Late Uruk period: Uruk is the leading city of southern Mesopotamia
Earliest unequivocal written documents (proto-cuneiform) appear at Uruk

journeys.name: Akkadian Empire
journeys.summary: Sargon of Akkad (r. c. 2334–2279 BCE) conquered Sumer and campaigned from the Gulf to Syria and Elam, creating the first empire to rule all Mesopotamia. His grandson Naram-Sin crushed a great revolt and took the realm to its widest extent, but after Shar-kali-sharri (d. c. 2193 BCE) the state broke apart under Gutian and Amorite pressure and fell c. 2154 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Sargon comes to power and founds a dynasty ruling from Akkad (site still unknown)
Sargon defeats Lugalzagesi in three battles, razes Uruk's walls and takes Sumer
Sargon takes Mari and claims the 'Upper Country' to the Cedar Forest

journeys.name: Third Dynasty of Ur (Neo-Sumerian Empire)
journeys.summary: After the Gutian interlude, Ur-Nammu of Ur (r. c. 2112–2094 BCE) reunited Sumer and Akkad, and his son Shulgi built a centralised, bureaucratic state of some twenty provinces ringed by a military periphery along the Zagros. Amorite incursions, revolts and the breakaway of Isin weakened his successors, and c. 2004 BCE an Elamite coalition sacked Ur. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Ur-Nammu takes power at Ur and founds the Third Dynasty
Ur-Nammu dies in battle in the eastern highlands; Shulgi begins a 48-year reign
Shulgi, a god by his 21st year, reforms weights, taxes and the bureaucracy

journeys.name: Old Babylonian Empire (Hammurabi)
journeys.summary: Hammurabi (r. c. 1792–1750 BCE) turned Babylon from one Amorite kingdom among many into the master of Mesopotamia, conquering Larsa, Mari and Eshnunna and issuing his famous law code. Under his son Samsu-iluna revolts wrecked the southern cities and the far south broke away as the Sealand dynasty; a shrunken kingdom lasted until the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon c. 1595 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

Hammurabi conquers Larsa and annexes Rim-Sin's kingdom in the south

journeys.name: Hittite Empire
journeys.summary: From their capital Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittite kings Hattusili I and Mursili I raided as far as Aleppo and Babylon (c. 1595 BCE) before the Old Kingdom sank into court strife. Suppiluliuma I (c. 1350–1322 BCE) broke Mitanni and made the Hittites masters of Syria; his successors fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and made peace. Around 1190 BCE, amid the wider Bronze Age collapse, Hattusa was abandoned and the empire vanished. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).

journeys.name: Egypt's New Kingdom empire
journeys.summary: Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos and reunited Egypt (c. 1549–1524 BCE); his successors, above all Thutmose III, built an empire from Nubia beyond the Fourth Cataract to the Euphrates. Egypt contested Syria with Mitanni and then the Hittites until the treaty of c. 1259 BCE, but after Ramesses III fought off the Sea Peoples its power ebbed, and by Ramesses XI's death in 1077 BCE the country was split between Tanis and Thebes. Reign dates follow the conventional low chronology and are approximate.

journeys.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
journeys.summary: From 911 BCE Assyrian kings reconquered northern Mesopotamia, and Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III made Assyria the dominant power of the Near East. After a long spell of weak kings, Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727 BCE) more than doubled the empire, and the Sargonid kings took Israel, Babylon and, in 671 BCE, Egypt. Within two decades of Ashurbanipal's death the Babylonians and Medes destroyed Assur (614), Nineveh (612) and the last Assyrian army at Harran (609).

journeys.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire (Nebuchadnezzar II)
journeys.summary: Nabopolassar threw off Assyrian rule in 626 BCE and, allied with the Medes, destroyed Assyria by 609 BCE. His son Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BCE) won Syria and the Levant at Carchemish, destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BCE and rebuilt Babylon in splendour. After his death three short reigns ended in Nabonidus, whose long absence in Arabia left Babylon exposed; Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BCE.

journeys.name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
journeys.summary: Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes in 550 BCE and took Lydia and Babylon; Cambyses added Egypt and Darius I pushed the frontier to the Indus and into Europe, ruling c. 5.5 million km², the largest empire yet seen. Defeats in Greece (490, 480–479 BCE) and the loss of Egypt (404–343 BCE) dented but did not break it; Alexander of Macedon destroyed it in 334–330 BCE.

journeys.name: Roman Republic and Empire
journeys.summary: The Roman Republic (from c. 509 BCE) conquered Italy, then defeated Carthage and the Hellenistic kingdoms to dominate the Mediterranean, before civil wars ended in one-man rule under Augustus (27 BCE). The Empire peaked under Trajan at about 5 million km² (117 CE), survived the crisis of the third century, and was split for good between East and West in 395. The Western half lost its provinces to Germanic peoples and ended when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476.

journeys.name: Empire of Alexander the Great
journeys.summary: Philip II (359–336 BCE) made Macedon the master of Greece; his son Alexander III conquered the whole Persian Empire and pushed on to the Indus before dying in Babylon in 323 BCE. His generals kept the empire nominally united under his half-brother and infant son, but after both were murdered they took royal titles, and the battle of Ipsus (301 BCE) fixed its partition into rival kingdoms.

journeys.name: Maurya Empire
journeys.summary: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda dynasty of Magadha c. 321 BCE and, after war with Seleucus I, won the lands up to the Hindu Kush. Bindusara pushed into the Deccan and Ashoka conquered Kalinga c. 261 BCE, ruling nearly all of South Asia except the far south before turning to Buddhism. After Ashoka's death in 232 BCE weaker kings followed, and the general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last, Brihadratha, c. 185 BCE.

journeys.name: Seleucid Empire
journeys.summary: Seleucus I took Babylon in 312 BCE and, after Ipsus and Corupedium, ruled from the Aegean to the borders of India. Bactria and Parthia broke away in the mid-3rd century; Antiochus III restored much of the realm but lost Anatolia to Rome after Magnesia (190 BCE), and the Parthians took Mesopotamia in 141 BCE. Reduced to Syria and torn by dynastic wars, the kingdom was annexed by Pompey in 63 BCE.

journeys.name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
journeys.summary: Ptolemy I, Alexander's satrap in Egypt from 323 BCE, made himself king in 305 BCE and added Cyrenaica, Cyprus and Coele-Syria; under Ptolemy III in the 240s the kingdom reached its height, campaigning as far as Babylonia. Native revolts, the loss of Coele-Syria (200 BCE) and dynastic feuds weakened it as Rome's influence grew; Cleopatra VII's defeat at Actium led to Egypt's annexation by Rome in 30 BCE.

journeys.name: Parthian Empire
journeys.summary: Arsaces I, leader of the Parni, founded the Arsacid state in Parthia c. 247 BCE; Mithridates I (c. 171–132 BCE) took Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids, and Mithridates II extended Parthian power from the Euphrates to Afghanistan. Astride the Silk Road, Parthia fought Rome for three centuries, destroying Crassus at Carrhae but losing Ctesiphon to Trajan, Avidius Cassius and Severus. Weakened by civil war, the last king, Artabanus IV, fell to Ardashir I of Persis in 224 CE.

journeys.name: Qin and Han China
journeys.summary: The state of Qin conquered its last rivals in 221 BCE and its king became the First Emperor, standardising script, coinage and law, but the dynasty collapsed in revolts soon after his death and ended in 206 BCE. Liu Bang founded the Han in 202 BCE; under Emperor Wu (141–87 BCE) it drove back the Xiongnu and expanded into Central Asia, Korea and the far south. After Wang Mang's Xin interlude (9–23 CE) the Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang until rebellion and warlords ended it in 220 CE.

journeys.name: Xiongnu
journeys.summary: Modu Chanyu (209–174 BCE) united the nomads of the Mongolian Plateau into a confederation that humbled the early Han and drove the Yuezhi west. Emperor Wu's wars from 133 BCE broke Xiongnu power; a succession war ended with Huhanye submitting to Han, and in 48 CE the confederation split into Southern and Northern Xiongnu. Han campaigns in 89–91 CE destroyed the Northern state, whose chanyu fled west.

journeys.name: Kushan Empire
journeys.summary: Kujula Kadphises united the Yuezhi tribes of Bactria in the 1st century CE, and his successors pushed into north-western India. Under Kanishka I (c. 127–150) the empire stretched from Central Asia to the Ganges plain, ruled from Purushapura and Mathura and linking the Silk Road, India and Rome. After Vasudeva I (d. c. 225) Sasanian Persia took the west, and the eastern 'Little Kushans' faded under Gupta suzerainty and the Kidarites by c. 375.

journeys.name: Sasanian Empire
journeys.summary: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians in 224 and his son Shapur I humiliated Rome, capturing the emperor Valerian in 260. For four centuries the Sasanians rivalled Rome and Byzantium; Khosrow I (531–579) sacked Antioch and took Yemen, and Khosrow II briefly held the Levant and Egypt. Exhausted by the war of 602–628 and the civil war that followed, the empire fell to the Arab conquests, ending with Yazdegerd III's death in 651.

journeys.name: Gupta Empire
journeys.summary: From the Gangetic plain, Chandragupta I (c. 319–335) raised the Gupta dynasty to imperial rank; Samudragupta's conquests and Chandragupta II's defeat of the Western Satraps made it the dominant power of northern India, a 'Golden Age' of art and science. Skandagupta repelled the Huns c. 455, but after him the empire lost ground to feudatories and to the Alchon Huns under Toramana and Mihirakula, and it had faded by the mid-6th century.

journeys.name: Hunnic Empire (Attila)
journeys.summary: Nomadic Huns crossed the Volga around 370, subdued the Alans and Goths and by the 420s were based on the Great Hungarian Plain, extorting tribute from both halves of the Roman Empire. Under Attila (sole ruler from c. 445) they ravaged the Balkans, Gaul and Italy, but after his death in 453 the subject peoples revolted at the Nedao and the empire fell apart; his son Dengizich was killed in 469.

journeys.name: Byzantine Empire
journeys.summary: The eastern half of the Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, outlived the West and under Justinian I reconquered North Africa, Italy and southern Spain, reaching its greatest extent in 565. The Arab conquests of the 630s–640s stripped away Syria and Egypt; the Macedonian emperors recovered ground up to Basil II's conquest of Bulgaria, before Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to the Turks. Sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 and restored from Nicaea in 1261, the shrunken state fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

journeys.name: Tang China
journeys.summary: Founded in 618 by Li Yuan amid the collapse of the Sui (the map starts in 623), the Tang destroyed the Eastern Turks, conquered the Tarim Basin and, with Silla, Goguryeo, pushing protectorates as far as Central Asia. Defeat at Talas (751) and the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) ended this expansion, after which Tibet and regional governors ate into Tang power. The Huang Chao rebellion devastated the empire and the last emperor was deposed in 907.

journeys.name: Tibetan Empire
journeys.summary: Under Songtsen Gampo (r. c. 618–650) the Yarlung kings united the Tibetan Plateau, moved their seat to Lhasa and absorbed Zhangzhung and the Tuyuhun. Tibet contested the Tarim Basin with Tang China for two centuries, briefly occupied Chang'an in 763 and reached its greatest extent in the early 800s. After the murder of Ralpachen (838) and the assassination of Langdarma in 842 the empire broke apart.

journeys.name: Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates
journeys.summary: After Muhammad's death in 632 the first caliphs, ruling from Medina, united Arabia and within twenty years took Syria and Egypt from Byzantium and destroyed the Sasanian Empire. From 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus and pushed the conquests to Spain, Sindh and Central Asia, creating one of the largest empires yet seen (c. 11 million km² by 720). Defeats at Constantinople (718) and Tours (732), the Berber revolt and civil wars sapped the dynasty, and the Abbasids overthrew it in 750.

journeys.name: Abbasid Caliphate
journeys.summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, founded Baghdad in 762 and under al-Mansur, Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun presided over a vast empire and a golden age of learning. From the 9th century provinces broke away (Aghlabids, Tahirids, Tulunids, then the Fatimids), and after 945 the caliphs were figureheads under the Buyids and then the Seljuks; the map shows no Abbasid territory between 970 and 1201. Caliph al-Nasir revived a small state in Iraq, but the Mongols sacked Baghdad and killed the last caliph in 1258.

journeys.name: Carolingian Empire (Charlemagne)
journeys.summary: Pepin the Short replaced the Merovingians as king of the Franks in 751, and his son Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom, Saxony and the Avar lands, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. After the civil war that followed Louis the Pious's death, the Treaty of Verdun (843) split the empire among his three sons. Charles the Fat reunited it in 884, but he was deposed in 887 and the empire dissolved for good on his death in 888.

journeys.name: Ghana Empire (Wagadu)
journeys.summary: The Soninke kingdom of Ghana, between the Senegal and Niger rivers, grew rich on the trans-Saharan gold trade and was already known to Arab writers as the 'Land of Gold' in the 8th century. It peaked in the 10th–11th centuries, seized the trading town of Awdaghust in 990 and was described in detail by al-Bakri in 1068. Its rulers converted to Islam around 1076 (whether the Almoravids conquered it is disputed); weakened, it was overrun by the Sosso by 1203 and later absorbed into Mali.

journeys.name: Khmer Empire
journeys.summary: Jayavarman II's consecration as universal monarch on Phnom Kulen in 802 founded the Angkorian empire, and Yasovarman I built the first capital at Angkor. Suryavarman II (builder of Angkor Wat) and Jayavarman VII (Angkor Thom, the Bayon) led its high point, including the conquest of Champa after the Cham sack of Angkor in 1177. From the 14th century the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya pressed in, and Angkor was abandoned after its fall in 1431.

journeys.name: Chola Empire
journeys.summary: Vijayalaya re-founded Chola power at Thanjavur around 848, and his successors overcame the Pandyas and Pallavas. Rajaraja I (985–1014) and Rajendra I (1014–1044) made it the leading power of South India and the Bay of Bengal, taking Sri Lanka and the Maldives, marching to the Ganges and raiding Srivijaya in 1025. The Later Cholas held most of the Tamil country after 1070, but Pandya attacks from 1215–16 broke the empire; the map ends in 1259, and the last king, Rajendra III, is last recorded in 1279.

journeys.name: Holy Roman Empire
journeys.summary: Otto I's imperial coronation in 962 joined the German kingdom to Italy, and Burgundy was added in 1032, making the empire the strongest monarchy in western Europe into the 13th century. Clashes with the papacy and the collapse of Hohenstaufen power after 1250 left the princes increasingly independent, a system fixed by the Golden Bull of 1356 and the reforms of 1495. The Reformation and the Thirty Years' War further weakened imperial authority; Westphalia (1648) recognised the loss of Switzerland and the Dutch Netherlands, and Francis II dissolved the empire in 1806.

journeys.name: Great Seljuk Empire
journeys.summary: Oghuz Turks led by Tughril and Chaghri took Merv and Nishapur in 1037–38, crushed the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan and in 1055 entered Baghdad as protectors of the Abbasid caliph. Alp Arslan's victory at Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia, and under Malik-Shah and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk the empire stretched from the Levant to Central Asia. After 1092 it fragmented among rival heirs; Sanjar's defeat at Qatwan (1141) and capture by the Oghuz (1153) ended Seljuk power in the east, and the last sultan fell to the Khwarazmians in 1194, leaving only the Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia (to 1308).

journeys.name: Mongol Empire
journeys.summary: Proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Temüjin united the steppe and conquered northern China and the Khwarazmian Empire; his successors took the Jin, Rus' and the Abbasid caliphate, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history. After Möngke's death in 1259 the Toluid civil war split the empire into the Yuan dynasty and three western khanates (the Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate and Ilkhanate). Kublai completed the conquest of Song China in 1279, but his attacks on Japan failed, and by his death in 1294 the four khanates went their own way.

journeys.name: Delhi Sultanate
journeys.summary: Founded in 1206 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak in the Indian lands of the Ghurids, the sultanate was ruled in turn by the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties. Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq pushed its armies deep into the south, briefly ruling most of the subcontinent, but rebellions created the Bahmani, Vijayanagara and other independent states. Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 left a small kingdom that the Lodis partly revived, until Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.

journeys.name: Mali Empire
journeys.summary: Sundiata Keita's victory over the Sosso at Kirina (c. 1235) founded the Mali Empire, which absorbed old Ghana and controlled the gold and salt trade of the western Sahel. It peaked in the 14th century under Mansa Musa, whose 1324 pilgrimage through Cairo became legendary, and Sulayman, whose court Ibn Battuta visited. After 1360 weak rulers, Tuareg and Mossi raids and the rise of Songhai cost it Timbuktu, Gao and the north; a last attempt to take Djenné failed in 1599 and the empire broke up after Mahmud IV's death c. 1610.

journeys.name: Ottoman Empire
journeys.summary: Founded c. 1299 by Osman I as a frontier principality in northwest Anatolia, the Ottoman state crossed into the Balkans, took Constantinople in 1453 and under Selim I and Suleiman I absorbed the Mamluk lands and most of Hungary. It reached its greatest extent around 1683, then lost ground to Habsburg Austria, Russia and Balkan nationalism over two centuries, and was dismantled after defeat in the First World War; the sultanate was abolished in 1922.

journeys.name: Aztec Empire
journeys.summary: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325, and served the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco until they overthrew them in 1428 and formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan. Under Itzcoatl, Moctezuma I, Axayacatl and Ahuitzotl the alliance built a tributary empire across central Mexico to the Gulf, Oaxaca and Soconusco, though it was halted by the Purépecha in the west. Cortés arrived in 1519 with Indigenous allies; after smallpox and a long siege, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521, after the map ends.

journeys.name: Timurid Empire
journeys.summary: Timur took control of the western Chagatai lands around 1370 (the map starts in 1375) and in three decades of campaigns conquered Iran and Iraq, broke the Golden Horde, sacked Delhi, Damascus and Baghdad and defeated the Ottomans at Ankara. After his death in 1405 his son Shah Rukh ruled from Herat over a smaller realm that saw the Timurid Renaissance. Civil wars, the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu cost the dynasty western Iran, and the Uzbeks took Samarkand (1501) and Herat (1507); Babur, a Timurid, went on to found the Mughal Empire.

journeys.name: Ming China
journeys.summary: The Hongwu Emperor proclaimed the Ming in 1368 after driving out the Mongol Yuan, and his successors pushed into Yunnan, Manchuria and, briefly, Vietnam, while Zheng He's fleets sailed to the Indian Ocean. After the Tumu disaster of 1449 the dynasty turned defensive behind the rebuilt Great Wall; fiscal crisis, rebellion and the rising Manchus brought the fall of Beijing in 1644, and Ming loyalist courts in the south held out until 1662.

journeys.name: Portuguese Empire
journeys.summary: Portugal's seizure of Ceuta in 1415 opened a century of exploration down the African coast that reached India in 1498 and Brazil in 1500, and a chain of fortified ports from Goa to Malacca. The Dutch took much of its Asian trade in the 17th century, and Brazil became independent in 1822; Portugal then turned to Africa and held on to Angola and Mozambique through the colonial wars of 1961–1974, decolonising after the Carnation Revolution (Macau was handed over in 1999).

journeys.name: Inca Empire
journeys.summary: After defeating the Chanka, Pachacuti (traditionally from 1438) turned the kingdom of Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, and he and his son Topa Inca conquered the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile, including the coastal kingdom of Chimor. At its height under Huayna Capac it was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Disease and a succession war between Huáscar and Atahualpa weakened it just as Pizarro arrived; Atahualpa was seized at Cajamarca in 1532 and executed in 1533, though Inca resistance continued at Vilcabamba until 1572.

journeys.name: Russian Empire (Muscovy, Tsardom and Empire)
journeys.summary: Ivan III gathered the Russian principalities under Moscow and threw off Tatar overlordship; Ivan IV took the title of tsar in 1547 and conquered the Volga khanates, opening the way for Cossacks and traders to cross Siberia to the Pacific within a century. Peter the Great's victory over Sweden made Russia an empire in 1721, and expansion into Poland, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Amur followed until it reached its greatest extent in the late 19th century, before defeat by Japan and the First World War brought revolution in 1917.

journeys.name: Songhai Empire
journeys.summary: From Gao, Sonni Ali (r. 1464–1492) turned Songhai into the Sahel's leading power, taking Timbuktu and Djenné and much of Mali's former territory. Askia Muhammad I, who seized power in 1493, reorganised the state, made a celebrated pilgrimage to Mecca and pushed its frontiers further. After his overthrow in 1528 civil wars weakened the empire, and in 1591 a Moroccan army with firearms routed the Songhai at Tondibi and sacked Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné.

journeys.summary: Castile and Aragon completed the conquest of Granada and sponsored Columbus in 1492; within two generations Spain had overthrown the Aztec and Inca states and spread from the Americas to the Philippines, and from 1580 to 1640 its king also ruled Portugal. The empire reached its greatest extent in the late 18th century, lost the American mainland in the wars of independence (1808–1826), and lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines in 1898; its last African territories were given up in 1956–1976.

journeys.name: Safavid Empire
journeys.summary: Ismail I, head of the Safavid Sufi order, was enthroned at Tabriz in 1501 and within a decade had conquered Iran and Iraq and imposed Twelver Shi'ism. Defeat at Chaldiran in 1514 fixed a long frontier war with the Ottomans; Abbas I (1587–1629) rebuilt the state from Isfahan and won back lost ground, but Afghan invaders took Isfahan in 1722 and Nader Shah ended the dynasty in 1736.

journeys.name: Mughal Empire
journeys.summary: Babur, a Timurid prince from Kabul, defeated the Delhi sultan at Panipat in 1526; his son Humayun lost the realm to Sher Shah Suri and won it back in 1555. Akbar and his successors built one of the largest states in Indian history, which reached its widest extent under Aurangzeb (d. 1707) after the conquest of the Deccan sultanates. It then fragmented under Maratha, Persian, Afghan and British pressure, and the British deposed the last emperor after the 1857 rebellion.

journeys.name: Dutch Colonial Empire
journeys.summary: The newly independent Dutch Republic built a commercial empire through the East India Company (VOC, 1602) and West India Company (1621), seizing Portuguese posts from Malacca to Ceylon and founding Batavia, New Amsterdam and the Cape Colony; it was at its height around 1652. Wars with England and France eroded it, but in the 19th century the Netherlands turned its foothold in the East Indies into a vast colony, lost to Japanese occupation in 1942 and to Indonesian independence in 1945–1949.

journeys.name: British Empire
journeys.summary: England's East India Company (1600) and its first American colonies grew into a worldwide empire of trading posts, settler colonies and conquests; the loss of the Thirteen Colonies in 1783 was offset by India, Australia, the Cape and footholds across Asia. Victory in the First World War added League of Nations mandates and the empire reached its largest extent around 1921, but the Dominions became self-governing, India won independence in 1947, and most remaining colonies followed by the 1960s; the handover of Hong Kong in 1997 is often taken as its end.

journeys.name: Qing China
journeys.summary: Nurhaci united the Jurchen (Manchu) tribes as the Later Jin in 1616, and his son Hong Taiji renamed the state Qing in 1636; in 1644 Manchu armies entered Beijing and went on to conquer all of Ming China, Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang. At its peak around 1790 the Qing ruled roughly 14.7 million km², but the Opium Wars, the Taiping Rebellion, unequal treaties and defeat by Japan weakened it, and the 1911 revolution brought the abdication of the last emperor in 1912.

journeys.name: Maratha Empire
journeys.summary: Shivaji, crowned Chhatrapati in 1674, carved a Maratha kingdom out of the Deccan and survived a long war with Aurangzeb (1680–1707). Under Chhatrapati Shahu the Peshwas of Pune led the confederacy north across Malwa to Delhi and Attock, reaching a peak of roughly 2.5 million km² around 1760, until the Afghan victory at Panipat in 1761. The Marathas recovered Delhi in 1771 but were defeated by the British East India Company in three wars, the last ending in 1818.

journeys.name: First French Empire (Napoleonic)
journeys.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte was proclaimed Emperor of the French in May 1804 and crowned that December. Victories over Austria, Prussia and Russia (1805–1807) let him annex territory directly to France and ring it with satellite kingdoms and confederations run by his relatives and allies, a system at its height around 1810–1812. The disastrous invasion of Russia in 1812 and defeat at Leipzig in 1813 broke it, and he abdicated in April 1814; his return in the Hundred Days ended at Waterloo in 1815.

journeys.name: Empire of Japan
journeys.summary: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 created a modernising, centralised Japan that absorbed Hokkaido and the Ryukyu Islands and then won Taiwan from China (1895), southern Sakhalin and the Kwantung lease from Russia (1905), and Korea (1910). Seizing Manchuria in 1931 and invading China in 1937, it struck at the United States and European colonies in 1941 and briefly ruled an empire of about 7.4 million km² in 1942, before defeat and surrender in 1945.

journeys.name: German Empire
journeys.summary: Proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871 after Prussia's victory over France, the German Empire united the German states outside Austria under the Prussian king as emperor. From 1884 it acquired colonies in Africa and the Pacific, the fourth-largest colonial empire of its day, and under Wilhelm II pursued world-power ambitions; defeat in the First World War, despite brief gains in the east in 1918, brought revolution, the emperor's abdication and the loss of all its colonies.

journeys.name: Soviet Union
journeys.summary: Formed in December 1922 by the Bolshevik-ruled republics that emerged from the Russian Civil War, the Soviet Union recovered most of the old empire's lands. The 1939 pact with Nazi Germany let it annex eastern Poland, the Baltic states and parts of Finland and Romania; it survived the German invasion of 1941, won in 1945 with further gains, and dominated Eastern Europe as a superpower. Economic stagnation, the Afghan war and Gorbachev's reforms led to the collapse of its satellites in 1989 and its own dissolution in December 1991.
